true_positives.golden_comment: The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Malformed input causes unhandled 500s; no HTTP method check

`appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse(req.body)` (line 31), `symmetricDecrypt(reqBody.keys, ...)` and the surrounding `JSON.parse` (lines 57–59) all throw on invalid input (bad body shape, wrong encryption key, non-JSON plaintext), producing an unhandled 500 with a stack trace instead of a 4xx response. The handler also accepts any HTTP method, so a GET (empty body) takes the same crash path. Wrap validation/decryption in try/catch and reject non-POST methods.

false_negatives.golden_comment: parseRefreshTokenResponse returns a Zod safeParse result ({ success, data, error }), not the credential key object. Persisting that as key stores the wrapper instead of the token payload; we should store the parsed data or use schema parse.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

false_positives.candidate:
Missing prisma import — file will not compile

The newly added refresh block calls `prisma.credential.update({ where: { id: credential.id }, ... })` at line 96, but the file's import list (lines 1–21) never imports `prisma` from `@calcom/prisma`. This is a TypeScript compile error (`Cannot find name 'prisma'`), so the package/build fails whenever this file is type-checked.

No tests for the credential-sync webhook or refresh-sync paths

The PR adds a security-sensitive endpoint that decrypts and overwrites user credentials, plus a new token-refresh code path in nine app integrations, and the author explicitly states no tests were added. Given the multiple mode-dependent behaviors (sync on/off, per-app response shapes), at minimum the webhook's auth/upsert logic and `refreshOAuthTokens`/`parseRefreshTokenResponse` need unit tests before merge.

Sync response expiry is discarded, and stored key loses refresh_token

After the refresh call, the code computes `responseBody.expiry_date = Math.round(Date.now() + (responseBody?.expires_in || 0) * 1000)` and then overwrites the entire stored credential key with `responseBody`. The sync endpoint contract is "access token and expiry date", not necessarily `expires_in`; if it returns anything else (e.g. `expiry_date`), that value is clobbered with ~now, so `isExpired` is always true and every `getToken()` call hits the sync endpoint again. The wholesale key replacement also drops `refresh_token` from the stored credential, so if syncing is later disabled the credential can no longer refresh.

Webex still enforces provider-specific token schema, rejecting sync-endpoint responses

Unlike zoom/google/office365calendar, the webex refresh path was not switched to `parseRefreshTokenResponse` — it still parses the response with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`, which requires `scope` and `token_type` string literals, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Per the PR's own contract the sync endpoint returns only an access token and an expiry, so in sync mode parsing always fails and `refreshAccessToken` rejects with "Invalid refreshed tokens were returned", making Webex meetings unusable whenever credential syncing is enabled.

Webhook secret compared with non-constant-time !==

The shared webhook secret is verified with a plain string `!==` comparison between the header value and `process.env.CALCOM_WEBHOOK_SECRET`. For a long-lived bearer secret protecting an endpoint that writes arbitrary credential keys for any user, this should use a constant-time comparison (e.g. `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) to avoid leaking the secret byte-by-byte through response timing.

true_positives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Case-sensitive duplicate/blacklist comparison lets duplicate attendees in and breaks the blacklist

The dedupe filter compares `guest === attendee.email` and `blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest)` with exact string equality. The blacklist entries are lowercased but `guest` is not, so `Foo@Bar.com` on the blacklist is never matched. Worse, if the booking already has attendee `foo@bar.com` and someone submits `Foo@Bar.com`, the filter passes and `createMany` inserts a second attendee row for the same person (email uniqueness in the DB is case-sensitive), producing duplicate attendees who then both receive emails and calendar updates. Emails should be normalized (trimmed/lowercased) before comparison and before insert.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isTeamAdminOrOwner uses && so it can never be true

In addGuests.handler.ts, `isTeamAdminOrOwner` is computed as `(await isTeamAdmin(user.id, teamId)) && (await isTeamOwner(user.id, teamId))`. A membership in Cal.com has a single role, so a user cannot simultaneously be ADMIN and OWNER of the same team — this expression is always false. As a result, team admins and team owners (whom the UI explicitly allows to manage the booking via `booking.isUserTeamAdminOrOwner` in BookingListItem) will always hit the FORBIDDEN branch and cannot add guests. The two checks should be combined with `||`.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Raw `guests` (not `uniqueGuests`) passed to sendAddGuestsEmails sends the wrong template

`sendAddGuestsEmails(evt, guests)` is called with the raw input array, not the deduplicated `uniqueGuests`. In email-manager.ts, each attendee gets the full `AttendeeScheduledEmail` if `newGuests.includes(attendee.email)`, otherwise the "guests added" notification. So if the requester includes an email that is already an attendee (filtered out of `uniqueGuests`, not re-added), that existing attendee incorrectly receives a brand-new booking confirmation email instead of the notification. Conversely, because the matching is case-sensitive, a genuinely new guest stored with different casing than the input gets the notification template instead of the confirmation. Pass `uniqueGuests` and compare normalized emails.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
sendAddGuestsEmails ignores event-type email opt-out settings

Every other send function in this file (sendScheduledEmails, sendLocationChangeEmails, sendCancelledEmails, etc.) accepts `eventTypeMetadata` and skips host/attendee emails when `disableStandardEmails.all.host/attendee` is set, and also strips `additionalNotes` when `hideCalendarNotes` is set. `sendAddGuestsEmails` takes no metadata parameter and unconditionally emails the organizer, all team members, and all attendees. Event types that disabled standard emails (a documented privacy feature, e.g. when workflows replace them) will still send these notifications, and hidden calendar notes can leak to attendees.

false_negatives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Attendees added to seated events without BookingSeat references

The handler copies `seatsPerTimeSlot`/`seatsShowAttendees` into the CalendarEvent, so seated event types reach this code, but it inserts attendees with a plain `createMany` and never creates the `BookingSeat` reference rows that seated bookings require to track occupancy and to let the attendee manage/reschedule their seat. For a seated event this corrupts seat accounting (the new attendee occupies no seat) and breaks flows that rely on `seatsReferences`. The handler should either reject bookings whose event type has `seatsPerTimeSlot` set, or create proper seat references.

Calendar update uses the caller's credentials instead of the organizer's

The handler builds the EventManager from `getUsersCredentials(ctx.user)` and `new EventManager({ ...user, credentials })`, i.e. the credentials and identity of whoever clicked "add guests". But the permission check explicitly allows attendees and team admins to call this endpoint, and the calendar event being updated belongs to the booking organizer (`booking.user`). When anyone other than the organizer adds guests, `eventManager.updateCalendarAttendees(evt, booking)` runs with credentials that have no access to the organizer's calendar, so the calendar event is never updated with the new attendees (or the call fails). Note the booking query already includes `booking.user.credentials` but they are never used — the organizer's credentials/user should be used to construct the EventManager.

No booking status check — guests can be added to cancelled, rejected, or past bookings

After fetching the booking, the handler only checks permissions; it never verifies `booking.status` or `booking.endTime`. The UI only shows the action for confirmed bookings, but the tRPC mutation is directly callable, so any attendee can add guests to a CANCELLED or REJECTED booking (or one that already ended), creating Attendee rows and triggering confirmation/ICS emails with method REQUEST for a dead event. The handler should reject bookings that are not ACCEPTED (and arguably those already in the past).

No upper bound on guests array enables email spam abuse

`guests: z.array(z.string().email())` has no `.max()` and no `.min(1)`. Since the handler permits any existing attendee (not just the organizer) to call this mutation, anyone who attended a booking can submit hundreds of arbitrary email addresses, creating hundreds of Attendee rows and causing Cal.com to send organizer-branded invitation emails (with ICS attachments and reply-to set to the organizer) to all of them. Add a reasonable `.max()` (and `.min(1)`) to the schema.

Validation error message never clears when the user edits emails

`isInvalidEmail` is set to true when validation fails, but nothing resets it when the user subsequently edits or removes email fields — it is only cleared on cancel or successful submit. A user who fixes the offending address still sees "Emails must be unique and valid" until they click Add again, which is confusing. Clear the flag in the `setValue` path (e.g. wrap `setMultiEmailValue` to also reset `isInvalidEmail`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Read-modify-write retryCount instead of atomic increment

Both retry updates use `retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1`, computed from the value read at the start of the run. If two cron executions overlap (this endpoint is triggered by an external cron and has no locking), both can read retryCount = 0 and both write 1, losing an increment and extending the retry loop beyond the intended two attempts. Prisma supports an atomic `retryCount: { increment: 1 }` which avoids the stale-read problem entirely. Same issue at line 195 in the catch block.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry-based deletion is not scoped to SMS reminders

The new second branch of the deleteMany OR ({ retryCount: { gt: 1 } }) has no `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` filter, unlike the first branch which is explicitly SMS-scoped. This cron endpoint is SMS-only (the file header says so and the fetch below only selects SMS reminders), but the delete will now remove ANY WorkflowReminder row with retryCount > 1, including EMAIL or WHATSAPP reminders. It also ignores the `scheduled` flag, so even an already-scheduled reminder with retryCount > 1 would be deleted. Today only this file increments retryCount (and only for SMS rows), so the impact is latent, but the moment any other scheduler (e.g., the email reminder cron) starts using retryCount, this job will silently delete those reminders. The retryCount condition should be ANDed with `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` (and probably `scheduled: false`).

false_positives.candidate:
Any transient error counts toward permanent deletion after only two attempts

The catch block wraps the entire per-reminder body, so retryCount is incremented for any failure — not just SMS scheduling failures. For example, a transient database hiccup in `prisma.profile.findFirst` (line 111) or `getBookerBaseUrl` (line 119) increments retryCount just the same as an invalid phone number. Combined with the hard deletion at retryCount > 1, two consecutive transient failures (e.g., a brief Twilio or DB outage spanning two cron runs) permanently delete reminders whose scheduledDate may still be days away and which would have succeeded on a later run. Consider only counting actual send failures, or using a higher threshold / not deleting reminders whose scheduledDate is still in the future.

Comment above deleteMany no longer matches the query

The comment still reads 'delete all scheduled sms reminders where scheduled date is past current date', but the query now also deletes unscheduled reminders (of any method) whose retryCount exceeds 1. The stale comment misleads future readers about what this cleanup does; it should be updated to describe both deletion conditions.

Unprotected prisma.update inside catch can abort the whole run

The catch block now performs `await prisma.workflowReminder.update({ where: { id: reminder.id }, ... })` without its own error handling. If that update itself throws — for example because the reminder row was deleted between the findMany and this update (the deleteMany at the top of a concurrent cron run can remove it), or because of a transient DB error — the exception escapes the catch, breaks out of the `for` loop entirely, and all remaining unscheduled reminders in the batch are skipped while the endpoint returns a 500. Previously the catch only logged, so one failing reminder never affected the rest of the batch. The increment in the catch should be wrapped in its own try/catch (or use updateMany which won't throw on a missing row).

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

false_positives.candidate:
Authorization/filter SQL fragments are returned unparenthesized, so ANDing extra predicates silently changes semantics

`getAuthorizationConditions()` for team/org scope returns a top-level `OR` expression like `("teamId" = ...) AND ("isTeamBooking" = true)) OR (("userId" = ANY(...)) AND ("isTeamBooking" = false)` with no outer parentheses, and `getBaseConditions()` returns that auth fragment bare whenever there are no filters (`return authConditions`). Likewise `getFilterConditions()` returns `("eventTypeId" = X) OR ("eventParentId" = X)` unwrapped. The old object-notation API merged conditions via Prisma `AND` arrays, so callers could safely add their own predicates; with the new raw-SQL API, any caller that writes `WHERE ${baseConditions} AND "createdAt" >= ...` (the natural way to add date-range filtering in insights) gets `A OR B AND ...` which parses as `A OR (B AND ...)`, silently broadening the result set beyond the authorized scope — a potential data-exposure bug. Wrap the final reduced auth and filter expressions in parentheses (e.g. `Prisma.sql`(${combined})``) so the fragments are safely composable.

Caching tests for authorization and filter conditions deleted while the caching code remains

The PR removes the entire "Caching" describe block ("should cache authorization conditions" and "should cache filter conditions") from the integration tests. The service still implements and relies on that behavior via `cachedAuthConditions` / `cachedFilterConditions` in `getAuthorizationConditions()` and `getFilterConditions()`. Rather than updating the two assertions to the new `Prisma.sql` format (they would only have needed the expected value changed, since the second call returning the cached object is format-agnostic), the coverage was dropped entirely, leaving the memoization logic untested. Restore equivalent tests asserting that a second call returns the identical cached `Prisma.Sql` instance.

Public findMany() method removed without migrating or even checking callers

The PR deletes the service's only data-access method, `findMany(findManyArgs)`, and replaces it with `getBaseConditions()`, which just returns a raw SQL fragment. It also changes the constructor's accepted options type from `InsightsBookingServiceOptions` to the new `InsightsBookingServicePublicOptions`. No other files are changed in this PR, so any existing consumer of `InsightsBookingService` (router, handler, repository, or an interface the class implements) that calls `.findMany(...)` will fail to compile, and consumers now have to hand-write `$queryRaw` queries themselves. Before merging, verify every caller of this service has been migrated (or keep a `findMany` that composes the raw query internally); if callers are migrated in a stacked PR, that dependency should be explicit, otherwise this is a breaking change.

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dev script uses macOS-only `sed -i ''` and a cwd-relative .env path

Two portability/correctness issues in the new helper script: (1) `sed -i '' -E ...` is BSD/macOS syntax — on GNU/Linux `sed -i ''` treats the empty string as a filename and the script fails with "can't read : No such file or directory", so the script silently breaks for Linux developers. (2) `ENV_FILE="../.env"` is resolved relative to the caller's current working directory, not the script's location; running it from anywhere other than the `scripts/` directory will create or modify a `.env` in an unintended parent directory. Resolve the env file relative to the script's own path (e.g. via `$(dirname "$0")`).

true_positives.golden_comment: Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
deleteCache handler throws a generic Error instead of a TRPCError

When the credential is not found or doesn't belong to the user, the handler does `throw new Error("Credential not found or access denied")`. tRPC converts a generic `Error` into an `INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR` (HTTP 500), so clients see a server error for what is actually a not-found/forbidden condition, and it may get reported as an unexpected server fault. Throw a `TRPCError` with code `NOT_FOUND` (or `FORBIDDEN`) to match the convention used elsewhere in the codebase.

true_positives.golden_comment: Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cache 'last updated' timestamp hardcoded to en-US locale

The cache status line formats the timestamp with `new Intl.DateTimeFormat("en-US", ...)`, ignoring the user's configured locale even though `useLocale()` is already available in the component. Non-US users will see US date/time formatting in a user-facing settings page, inconsistent with the rest of the app. Pass the user's locale (e.g. `i18n.language` from `useLocale`) or use the app's existing date-formatting helpers.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

false_positives.candidate:
Unconditional empty updateMany write to bump SelectedCalendar.updatedAt whose value is never read

`fetchAvailabilityAndSetCache` now ends with `await SelectedCalendarRepository.updateManyByCredentialId(this.credential.id, {})`, an `updateMany` with empty data whose only effect is to touch `updatedAt` on every SelectedCalendar row for the credential. This runs on the webhook/cache-refresh hot path, yet the PR description itself notes that `SelectedCalendar.updatedAt` is not displayed or read anywhere (the UI uses `CalendarCache.updatedAt` via `cacheUpdatedAt`). This is a dead write on a hot path; either remove it or wire it to an actual consumer before merging. Additionally, the method's parameter is typed `Prisma.SelectedCalendarUpdateInput` while `updateMany` expects `SelectedCalendarUpdateManyMutationInput` — it only compiles because `{}` is passed; any real payload with relation fields would be a type error.

UserWithCalendars type widened to require updatedAt/googleChannelId that nothing in this module consumes

`UserWithCalendars` now requires `updatedAt` and `googleChannelId` on both `allSelectedCalendars` and `userLevelSelectedCalendars`, but neither field is read anywhere in `getConnectedDestinationCalendarsAndEnsureDefaultsInDb` or its helpers in this file (the only consumer of the new `updatedAt` write is the frontend reading `CalendarCache.updatedAt` instead, per the PR's own notes). Only `findUnlockedUserForSession` was updated to select the new fields; any other caller of this widely-used function (it is re-exported as `getConnectedDestinationCalendars` for `@calcom/platform-libraries`, plus tests/fixtures constructing this type) that builds the user object without these fields will now fail type-checking. Either consume the fields or revert the type widening to avoid a needless contract break.

connectedCalendars handler bypasses the feature-flag/mock and queries calendarCache unconditionally

The handler instantiates `new CalendarCacheRepository()` directly and calls `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` on every `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` query. Everywhere else in the codebase the repository is obtained via `CalendarCache.init(null)`, which returns `CalendarCacheRepositoryMock` when the calendar-cache feature flag is disabled. By constructing the repository directly, this handler (a) runs an extra `groupBy` query against the `CalendarCache` table on every calendar-settings page load even for instances/teams where the feature is off, and (b) makes the newly added `getCacheStatusByCredentialIds()` implementation on the mock dead code — the mock will never be consulted here. Use the same init/feature-flag path as the rest of the calendar-cache code so the query is skipped when the feature is disabled.

true_positives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Reminder-cancellation calls are fire-and-forget; the cancelled flag may never be persisted

In the cancellation flow, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` and `deleteScheduledSMSReminder(reminder.id, reminder.referenceId)` are invoked inside `Array.forEach` without being awaited. The whole fix depends on the `workflowReminder.update({ data: { cancelled: true } })` (or row delete) inside those async functions actually completing. The previous implementation collected the Prisma `deleteMany` promises and awaited them in `Promise.all`; now nothing is awaited, so the handler can return (and on serverless platforms like Vercel the function can be frozen) before the DB writes run, silently leaving reminders un-cancelled — the exact bug this PR fixes. The same un-awaited pattern was introduced at the other call sites: `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/bookings.tsx` (requestReschedule, ~line 490), `packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts` (~line 966) and `packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/workflows.tsx` (lines 212-218, 376-382, 519-525, 574-580). These should be collected into an array of promises and awaited.

true_positives.golden_comment: When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
immediateDelete path cancels in SendGrid but leaves stale DB rows and long-lived pending cancellations

When `immediateDelete` is true, `deleteScheduledEmailReminder` only POSTs the cancel to SendGrid and returns — it neither deletes the `WorkflowReminder` row nor sets `cancelled: true`. For the workflow-delete and step-delete callers this is masked by the DB cascade, but in the reschedule path (`packages/features/bookings/lib/handleNewBooking.ts` line 968) the old booking's reminder rows stay in the database with `scheduled=true`, `cancelled=null` until their `scheduledDate` passes and the cron's past-date `deleteMany` happens to remove them. Worse, the reschedule path still cancels immediately in SendGrid for sends up to 72h out, and per the PR description such pending cancellations sit in SendGrid's `scheduled_sends` until the scheduled date and count toward the 100-pending-cancellations limit — the exact limit whose exhaustion caused this bug. Reschedules should use the same deferred mechanism (set `cancelled=true`, let the cron cancel within the final hour, and delete/flag the row) instead of `immediateDelete`.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

false_positives.candidate:
One failing SendGrid request aborts cancellation of all remaining reminders in that cron run

In the new cancellation block, the `for` loop awaits `client.request(...)` sequentially, and any thrown error breaks out of the loop into the outer `catch`, skipping all not-yet-processed reminders in `remindersToCancel`. Additionally, the Prisma delete promises already accumulated for successfully cancelled reminders are never awaited in that case, so those rows are not deleted either (Prisma promises are lazy and only execute when awaited). This self-heals on the next cron run only as long as the reminders' `scheduledDate` has not passed; a reminder near the end of its 1-hour window whose cancellation request repeatedly fails (or is unlucky behind a failing one) will be sent by SendGrid. Consider wrapping each reminder's cancel+delete in its own try/catch so one failure doesn't affect the rest.

true_positives.golden_comment: Consider adding try-catch around the await to handle import failures gracefully
true_positives.matched_candidate:
requestReschedule deletes calendar/video events in an un-awaited async forEach

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now awaits `getCalendar` inside the callback. `forEach` does not wait for async callbacks, so the mutation sends the reschedule email, fires the BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks, and returns while the calendar event deletions (`calendar.deleteEvent`) and video deletions (`deleteMeeting`) may still be in flight — and any failure (e.g. the dynamic import rejecting) surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection with no logging or error handling at all, since there is no try/catch here. Previously at least `getCalendar` was synchronous so its errors propagated to the caller. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)` (ideally with per-item error handling) before returning.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
async forEach makes the surrounding try/catch dead and deletions fire-and-forget

The change turns `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach((bookingRef) => {...})` into `forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` so `getCalendar` can be awaited. Because `forEach` never awaits async callbacks, (1) the surrounding `try/catch` (lines 124-139) can no longer catch any error thrown after the first await — a failed dynamic import or a rejected `deleteEvent`/`deleteMeeting` now escapes as an unhandled promise rejection, which on Node's default settings can terminate the server process; (2) the function proceeds to `sendRequestRescheduleEmail` and `return true` without waiting for the calendar/video deletions, so on serverless the response may complete (and the function be frozen) before the old events are removed, leaving stale events on attendees' calendars. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` and keep the try/catch around it.

false_positives.candidate:
Dynamic imports are evaluated eagerly, so all app bundles still load at startup

The object literal `const appStore = { applecalendar: import("./applecalendar"), ... }` evaluates every `import()` call as soon as `@calcom/app-store` itself is imported, so all ~28 app chunks begin loading immediately for any process that touches this module — the same startup cost as the previous static imports, just with extra microtask hops. If the intent of the PR is to defer loading apps until they are actually used, this does not achieve it; the values should be thunks, e.g. `applecalendar: () => import("./applecalendar")`, with call sites invoking the function. As written the change adds async complexity to every consumer without the advertised loading benefit.

async forEach makes the surrounding try/catch dead and deletions fire-and-forget

Identical to the vital app: `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` was introduced to await the now-async `getCalendar`. `forEach` does not await async callbacks, so the `try/catch` around it (lines 124-139) is now dead code for anything that happens after the first `await`, and any rejection from `getCalendar`, `calendar.deleteEvent`, or `deleteMeeting` becomes an unhandled promise rejection. Additionally the reschedule email is sent and `true` returned before the deletions finish, so a failed or incomplete cleanup is silently ignored. Replace with `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(...))`.

requestReschedule deletes calendar/video events in an un-awaited async forEach

In the `requestReschedule` mutation, `bookingRefsFiltered.forEach(async (bookingRef) => {...})` now awaits `getCalendar` inside the callback. `forEach` does not wait for async callbacks, so the mutation sends the reschedule email, fires the BOOKING_CANCELLED webhooks, and returns while the calendar event deletions (`calendar.deleteEvent`) and video deletions (`deleteMeeting`) may still be in flight — and any failure (e.g. the dynamic import rejecting) surfaces as an unhandled promise rejection with no logging or error handling at all, since there is no try/catch here. Previously at least `getCalendar` was synchronous so its errors propagated to the caller. Collect the promises and `await Promise.all(...)` (ideally with per-item error handling) before returning.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Working-hours check compares slot start against itself instead of slot end

In the new workingHours validation inside checkIfIsAvailable, both `start` and `end` are computed from `slotStartTime`: `const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`. This was clearly meant to be `slotEndTime` (slot start + eventLength). As written, a slot that starts inside working hours but ends after the working-hours end (e.g. a 60-minute slot starting 30 minutes before the end of a fixed host's availability) is treated as within hours and kept. Consequence: bookings can be created that extend past the fixed host's availability boundary, which is exactly the class of bug this PR is trying to fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Dayjs objects compared with === is always false

`dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes') === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, 'minutes')` compares two distinct dayjs object references and can never be true; the intended check for a full-day 'unavailable' override (start equals end) never fires. This is currently masked for 00:00-00:00 blocked days because the later `slotStartTime.isAfter(end)` check catches them, but a blocked-day override stored with any non-midnight equal start/end (or a slot spanning that point) will incorrectly be treated as available. Use `.isSame(...)` instead of `===`.

false_positives.candidate:
Host with no working hours on the slot's weekday is treated as available

The new workingHours check in checkIfIsAvailable only returns a match (and thus rejects the slot) when a workingHour exists whose `days` includes the slot's day AND the slot is outside its times. If the host has no working hour entry at all for that weekday (e.g. a fixed host who works Mon-Fri only, while the aggregated round-robin availability still produces Saturday slots from the other host's hours), `workingHours.find(...)` returns undefined, the check is skipped, and the slot passes as long as the host isn't busy. Consequence: fixed hosts remain bookable on days they don't work at all — the new enforcement only covers days where the host has partial hours. The check should reject the slot when no working hour covers that day.

Multiple date overrides on the same day make all slots unavailable

The `dateOverrides.find(...)` callback returns `true` (meaning 'block this slot') as soon as the slot is outside the time range of the first override matching the day, and `find` short-circuits without examining the remaining overrides. If a host has two override ranges on the same date (e.g. 09:00-11:00 and 14:00-16:00, which cal.com allows as separate availability rows for one date), a slot at 15:00 is outside the 09:00-11:00 range so the callback returns true and the slot is blocked; conversely any slot inside one range is outside the other, so every slot on that day ends up blocked. Consequence: days with more than one override range incorrectly show zero availability.

No test covers the fixed-host round-robin scenario the PR claims to fix

The PR description states its primary fix is that date overrides of fixed hosts are respected for round-robin events, and all of the new checkIfIsAvailable logic (date-override filtering per fixed host, working-hours bounds, organizerTimeZone plumbing) serves that path. The added test only extends the existing personal single-user event 'Check for Date overrides' test with a second invitee timezone; there is no scenario with a ROUND_ROBIN event type, hosts with isFixed, or a fixed host's date override. The bugs in that new code path (busy times skipped inside overrides, slot end never checked against working-hours end, hosts with no hours on a weekday treated as available) would not be caught by the current suite.

Override day matching formats the override date in the server's local timezone but the slot in UTC

The day comparison uses `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').format('YYYY MM DD')` — `dayjs(Date)` is in local mode, so `format` renders in the Node server's local timezone — and compares it to `slotStartTime.format('YYYY MM DD')` where `slotStartTime` is explicitly `.utc()`. On any server not running in UTC, the override start instant shifted by the organizer offset can format to a different calendar date than its UTC date, so date overrides silently fail to match (or match the wrong day). The code only works because production/test servers happen to run in UTC. Use `dayjs.utc(date.start)` (or `.tz(organizerTimeZone)`) consistently for this comparison.

Override timezone shift wraps across midnight and lands on the wrong day/hours

The new conversion computes startTime/endTime as `dayjs(override.start).utc().add(offset, 'minute').hour() * 60 + ...minute()`. When the organizer-to-invitee offset shift moves the override across midnight (e.g. organizer in UTC+5:30 with a 00:30-02:00 override, invitee in UTC: offset = -330 minutes, shifting to 18:30-20:00 of the previous day), `.hour()` silently wraps to the previous/next day's wall-clock hours while the `activeOverrides` filter on line 207 still applies the override to the invitee day matching the override's own date. Result: slots are generated at wrong times on the wrong invitee day (and in some cases startTime > endTime, producing no or inverted ranges) whenever a date override crosses midnight after timezone conversion.

Slots inside a date override skip the busy-time check, allowing double bookings

In checkIfIsAvailable, the new code returns early: if a date override exists for the slot's day and the slot falls within the override range, `dateOverrideExist` is true and the function returns `true` (available) at line 133-135 before ever reaching the `busy.every(...)` conflict check at the bottom. Since checkIfIsAvailable is the only place a fixed host's busy times/bookings are consulted, any existing booking or calendar busy time that falls inside a date-override window is ignored, and the slot is shown as bookable. Consequence: fixed hosts (and round-robin hosts via the looseHostAvailability path, which spreads the same schedule object) can be double-booked on days that have a date override. The busy check must still run when the slot is inside an override.

override.timeZone is optional in the type but used unconditionally

packages/types/schedule.d.ts declares `timeZone?: string` as optional on TimeRange, but getSlots now calls `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone)` without a fallback. When a caller passes date overrides without a timeZone, dayjs falls back to the server's guessed local timezone, so `organizerUtcOffset` — and therefore the shifted startTime/endTime — is computed against the wrong zone and the override is applied at incorrect times. Either make timeZone required on the override type or default it (e.g. to organizerTimeZone) before computing the offset.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test_basic function in test_consumer.py uses a monkeypatched time.sleep that returns immediately, but then calls time.sleep(0.1) expecting it to actually wait.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The added time.sleep(0.1) is a no-op because time.sleep is monkeypatched, leaving the race it was meant to fix

In `test_basic`, `monkeypatch.setattr("time.sleep", lambda _: None)` is applied at the top of the test, so the newly added `time.sleep(0.1)` (with the comment 'Give flusher threads time to process after drift change') resolves to the patched no-op and does not actually wait. The race it was intended to close is still present: `step.join()` sets `stopped.value = True` immediately, so if the flusher thread has not run a loop iteration between `fac._flusher.current_drift.value = 9000` and `join()`, it exits without flushing and `(msg,) = messages` fails. The test will be flaky under thread scheduling jitter. Either capture the real `time.sleep` before monkeypatching and call that, or poll until `messages` is non-empty with a real deadline.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because flusher processes are created via multiprocessing.get_context('spawn').Process, they are instances of multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess, which on POSIX is not a subclass of multiprocessing.Process, so this isinstance check will always be false and hung processes won't be killed here.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
isinstance check against multiprocessing.Process never matches spawn processes, so hung flusher processes are never killed

Flusher processes are created via `self.mp_context.Process`, where `mp_context = multiprocessing.get_context('spawn')`, so they are instances of `multiprocessing.context.SpawnProcess`. On Linux, `multiprocessing.Process` resolves to the default (fork) context's `ForkProcess` class — a sibling of `SpawnProcess`, not a parent — so `isinstance(process, multiprocessing.Process)` in `_ensure_processes_alive` is always False and `process.kill()` is never executed. Previously `kill()` was called unconditionally (guarded only by try/except ValueError), so this is a regression. Consequence: when a flusher process hangs (still alive but not updating `healthy_since`), the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` starts a new process for those shards without killing the old one, leaving two processes flushing the same shards concurrently — producing duplicate segments to the buffered-segments topic and racing on `done_flush_segments`. The same incorrect guard at line 346 in `join()` means `process.terminate()` is also silently skipped for spawn processes, so the shutdown fallback never force-terminates them. Use `multiprocessing.context.BaseProcess` (or `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`) for the isinstance check instead.

false_positives.candidate:
_create_process_for_shard is dead code

`_create_process_for_shard(self, shard)` is introduced in this PR but never called anywhere — the restart path in `_ensure_processes_alive` calls `_create_process_for_shards` directly.
