false_negatives.golden_comment: The magic number 50 for max_wait is used repeatedly throughout the tests. Consider extracting this as a named constant to improve maintainability.
The test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling has a docstring that doesn't match the test implementation.

false_positives.candidate:
Per-message metrics.gauge and per-message Sentry transaction with worker_id in the name add heavy per-message overhead

OrderedQueueWorker.run emits a metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth', ...) for every single processed message, and wraps every message in a sentry_sdk transaction whose name includes the worker_id (f"monitors.{identifier}.worker_{worker_id}"). On a high-throughput results topic this generates a gauge emission per message (the existing batched mode only emits per batch) and creates high-cardinality transaction names (one per worker per consumer) that won't group in Sentry Performance. Consider sampling, emitting gauges only from poll(), and removing worker_id from the transaction name.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite the docstring claiming it

FixedQueuePool creates each work queue with a bare queue.Queue() (maxsize=0, i.e. unbounded), and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit/poll never block or pause consumption. The class docstring for SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy claims 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', but submit() can never block, so if processing is slower than ingestion (the exact slow-item scenario this PR is meant to address) the consumer will read ahead without limit and buffer an unbounded number of decoded messages in process memory, risking OOM. Either give the queues a maxsize (making put block and naturally pause the consumer) or implement an explicit pause/resume in poll(), and fix the docstring if unbounded is intentional.

Strategy close() permanently kills the factory-owned queue pool, breaking the consumer after any rebalance and silently dropping messages

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), but the queue_pool is owned by ResultsStrategyFactory and is reused across partition assignments. On a partition revocation, arroyo calls close()/join() on the strategy, which sets worker.shutdown = True and calls q.shutdown() on every queue, so all worker threads exit and the queues are permanently shut down. When partitions are reassigned, the factory's create_thread_queue_parallel_worker (result_consumer.py) calls create_with_partitions again; its `assert self.queue_pool is not None` passes because only factory.shutdown() sets it to None, so a new SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy is built around a dead pool. Every subsequent submit() then calls queue.put() on a shut-down queue, which raises queue.ShutDown; that exception is caught by the broad `except Exception` in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit, which marks the offset complete — so the offset gets committed even though the message was never processed. The net effect after any routine rebalance (deploy, scaling event): the consumer silently drops all messages and keeps committing offsets, appearing healthy while processing nothing. The pool should either be recreated per create_with_partitions call or its lifecycle should be decoupled from the strategy's close().

Worker marks offsets complete even when processing raises, so failed messages are committed and lost

In OrderedQueueWorker.run, the finally block unconditionally calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(work_item.partition, work_item.offset), including when result_processor raised an exception that was caught by `except Exception`. Once the offset is marked complete, the commit loop will commit past it, and the failed message is never retried — a transient error causes permanent message loss. This also directly contradicts the new test test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling in tests/sentry/uptime/consumers/test_results_consumer.py, which asserts that no offset is committed when a message fails. If at-least-once semantics are intended (as the rest of the offset-tracking design suggests), complete_offset should only be called on success, and failures should either leave the offset outstanding or route to a DLQ.

join() ignores its timeout and close() abandons queued items without draining

SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.join(timeout) ignores the timeout parameter and just calls close(), which immediately shuts down the commit thread and the queue pool. FixedQueuePool.shutdown sets worker.shutdown = True before draining, so the workers' `while not self.shutdown` loop exits even when items remain in the queues; the existing wait_until_empty() helper is never used in any production path. On graceful shutdown, in-flight queued work is simply abandoned (it will be redelivered since offsets are not committed, but the class docstring's 'No item is lost' guarantee and the arroyo join contract — wait up to timeout for in-flight work to finish — are not honored, and the final processed-but-uncommitted offsets are not flushed, causing avoidable duplicate processing on every restart).

test_stats_reporting races with worker threads and is flaky

After submitting 10 work items to a pool whose 3 worker threads are actively draining, the test immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. If the workers process all items before get_stats() runs (likely on a fast machine since the result_processor is trivial), total_items will be 0 and the assertion fails nondeterministically. The test should block the processor (e.g. with an event) before checking queue depth, or drop the assertion.

test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behavior the implementation doesn't have and only passes due to commit-loop timing

The test mocks the result processor to raise on the first message and asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. But the implementation in OrderedQueueWorker.run completes offsets in a finally block even when processing raises, so both offsets become committable and the commit loop will commit offset 102. The test only passes because the commit thread waits 1.0s before its first commit and the test finishes (including its extra time.sleep(0.2)) well before that on a fast machine; under load or with a different commit interval it becomes flaky, and worse, it encodes the exact opposite of the real behavior, masking the message-loss issue where failed items are committed.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-precedence test uses a non-allowing cache entry, so it doesn't prove what its comment claims

In TestService_CacheCheck/"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry", the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the perm cache is seeded with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. Because checkPermission tests the truthiness of scopeMap[scope], a false value does not grant access, so this test would pass even if the denial cache were checked after the permission cache, or if the permission cache were consulted and simply found nothing allowing. To actually pin down the precedence behavior (denial cache wins over an allowing perm cache entry), the cached value must be true — which would currently fail and exposes the stale-denial-overrides-fresh-allow problem in Check.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The Check operation exhibits asymmetric cache trust logic: cached permission grants are trusted and returned immediately, but cached denials from the same permission cache are ignored, leading to a fresh database lookup. This allows stale cached grants to provide access to revoked resources, posing a security risk.

The cache key construction in `userPermDenialCacheKey` uses simple string concatenation with underscores, which can lead to ambiguous keys and collision risks when any component contains underscores or is empty. This could result in incorrect denial cache hits, affecting user permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Stale denial-cache entries take precedence over fresher positive permission data

In Check, the permission denial cache is consulted before the positive permission cache, and denial entries are never invalidated when the permission cache is refreshed. Sequence: (1) Check(user, dashboards:read, dash1) misses the perm cache, the DB requery denies, and a denial entry is cached (30s TTL). (2) The user is then granted read on dash1. (3) Any other Check for this user+action that falls through to the DB (e.g. for dash2) refreshes permCache via getUserPermissions with fresh data that now includes dash1. (4) A retry of Check(user, dashboards:read, dash1) hits the stale denial entry at line 117 and returns denied, even though the server's own freshly cached permission set says allow. The denial check should run after the positive cache check (allow on cached hit, then denial cache, then DB fallback), or denial entries for the user+action should be dropped when permCache is rewritten. As written, users can be denied access to just-granted resources for up to the full 30s TTL even when the server already holds fresh permissions proving the grant — which partially defeats the stated purpose of this PR (immediately accessing newly granted/created resources).

permissionCacheUsage metric recorded as a miss on a permission-cache hit that didn't grant access

When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission set but checkPermission does not allow the request (triggering the intended DB requery fallback), execution reaches line 137 and increments permissionCacheUsage with label "false" (miss), even though the permission cache was hit. Before this change the metric was incremented inside getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions strictly according to cache hit/miss, so dashboards and alerts built on the hit ratio will now show a drop in hit rate that does not reflect actual cache effectiveness. The hit should be recorded before evaluating checkPermission, with a separate metric (or label) for the fallback-to-DB path.

true_positives.golden_comment: The rendered GrafanaRuleListItem is missing the required key prop for React list items. This can cause rendering issues when the list order changes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
GrafanaRuleListItem rendered without a React key in the filtered rules list

In the `origin === 'grafana'` branch of the rules map, `<GrafanaRuleListItem>` is returned without `key={key}`, while the previous code passed `key={key}` to `GrafanaRuleLoader` and the sibling branches (`datasource`, `default`) still pass their keys. The component computes a stable `key` per rule precisely to avoid key duplication in this list. Rendering list children without keys triggers React's missing-key warning and, more importantly, can mis-associate component state (e.g. the delete modal / silence drawer state held by `RuleActionsButtons`) with the wrong rule row when pages are appended or the list is re-rendered. Add `key={key}` to the `GrafanaRuleListItem` element.

true_positives.golden_comment: RuleActionsButtons is invoked with only promRule, but SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer inside RuleActionsButtons still depends on a Grafana Ruler rule being present, so for Grafana rules coming from list views the 'Silence notifications' menu entry (now driven by Grafana Prom abilities) will toggle showSilenceDrawer without ever rendering the drawer. This means clicking 'Silence notifications' for these rules has no visible effect, even when abilities indicate silencing is allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Silence menu item is shown in the list view but clicking it does nothing

The silence drawer is only rendered when `rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)` is truthy: `{rulerRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule) && showSilenceDrawer && (<SilenceGrafanaRuleDrawer rulerRule={rule} .../>)}`. In the new list view only `promRule` is supplied (ruler API calls were removed), so `rule` is undefined. Meanwhile `AlertRuleMenu` now shows the 'Silence notifications' item based on prom-rule-based `canSilence`, and `handleSilence` sets `showSilenceDrawer(true)` — but no drawer ever mounts. The user clicks the menu item and nothing happens. Either gate the silence menu item on the presence of a ruler rule, or make the drawer work from the prom rule data.

false_positives.candidate:
Delete menu item can never appear in the rule list because it still requires a rulerRule

The Delete menu item is gated on `{canDelete && rulerRule && (...)}`. This PR computes `canDelete` from prom-rule-based abilities (`useGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`) specifically so delete works in the list view where 'we have removed all requests to the ruler API', but in that context `rulerRule` is always `undefined`, so the item never renders even when `grafanaDeleteSupported && grafanaDeleteAllowed` is true. The delete flow itself does not need the ruler rule — `RuleActionsButtons.V2` implements `handleDelete` as `() => showDeleteModal(identifier, groupIdentifier)`, which only uses the identifier. Net effect: users with delete permission cannot delete Grafana rules from the new list view (the updated GrafanaGroupLoader test even codifies this by expecting only 4 menu items with no Delete). Either drop the `rulerRule` requirement from the render guard or pass the identifier through instead.

ModifyExport ability for Grafana prom rules excludes recording rules, removing Export from the list view

In `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, `[AlertRuleAction.ModifyExport]: [isAlertingRule, exportAllowed]` uses `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`, which is false for recording rules. The ruler-based equivalent used `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` (`isGrafanaRulerRule`), which is true for both alerting and recording rules. In the list view (no ruler rule available), `canExport` therefore becomes false for Grafana-managed recording rules and the Export menu item disappears, whereas previously recording rules could be exported from the list. The same `isAlertingRule` gating on Pause/Restore also diverges from the old semantics (Grafana recording rules support pausing). Use a check that includes recording rules where the action legitimately applies to them.

Refactor of useAllAlertRuleAbilities drops the federated-rule-group immutability check

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (still used by existing components such as the old list's RuleActionsButtons via `useAlertRuleAbility`) previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and treated federated groups as immutable (no edit/delete). It now delegates to `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`, which hardcodes `const isFederated = false;` with a TODO, and the `isFederatedRuleGroup` import was removed. As a result, rules in federated Mimir rule groups (groups with `source_tenants`) are no longer marked immutable on this code path, so Edit/Delete buttons can be shown for rules that must not be modified through Grafana. Restore the federated check for the CombinedRule-based path or thread the group's `source_tenants` into `useAllRulerRuleAbilities`.

Rule view link no longer carries the returnTo parameter

The previous implementation built the rule link as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`; the new `GrafanaRuleListItem` drops the `returnTo` parameter. Users navigating from the list to a rule's detail page will lose the 'return to previous' context, so going back from the detail view no longer returns them to their filtered list position. If this was not an intentional product change, restore the `returnTo` query parameter.

Stale comment and variable name still reference ruler rule preloading

The comment above the cache-preload block still says 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded', and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`, but the `alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)` call was removed in this PR. The comment now describes behavior the code no longer has and is misleading to future readers; update the comment and rename the variable to reflect that only the Prometheus groups cache is populated.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

false_positives.candidate:
Ad hoc filters are now injected multiple times into split queries

applyTemplateVariables is now called with request.filters as the third argument, which injects the ad hoc filter matchers into the selector at split-preparation time. However, every split sub-request is still executed through datasource.runQuery, which applies the same request.filters to its targets again when it calls applyTemplateVariables. In the shard-splitting path it is even worse: runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) applies the filters, then runSplitQuery applies them again, then runQuery applies them a third time. With ad hoc filters configured and query splitting enabled, the expression sent to Loki contains the filter matchers duplicated two or three times, e.g. {job="x", cluster="us", cluster="us"}. This is semantically redundant, changes the query text (and therefore cache keys/history) compared to before this PR, and stacks multiple string-level insertions through the naive addAdhocFilters replacement. Filters should be applied in exactly one place in the execution chain.

Interpolating before the split decision defeats the $__range guard, so $__range queries are now split

runSplitQuery now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before partition() calls querySupportsSplitting(). querySupportsSplitting (line 287) relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) matching the literal '$__range' in the raw expression to exclude those queries from time-based splitting — the comment above it states these queries must not be split because the range window would be computed incorrectly per chunk. Because applyTemplateVariables runs templateSrv.replace over the expression, '$__range' is resolved to a fixed duration (the full request range) before the check executes, so isQueryWithRangeVariable can never match anymore and queries like avg_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) or topk(...)[$__range] are now split into per-day chunks, each chunk carrying the same pre-baked full-range window. This silently produces incorrect merged results for exactly the class of queries the guard was created to protect. The split/non-split decision must be made on the original uninterpolated expression (e.g., partition before applying template variables, or check isQueryWithRangeVariable on the pre-interpolation expr).

No test that $__range queries remain excluded from splitting

The new tests only cover the happy path (variables like $__auto and $step are replaced before execution). The behavior most at risk from moving interpolation to the start of runSplitQuery — that queries containing '$__range' are still routed to the non-splitting path via querySupportsSplitting — has no coverage, and in fact no longer works. A test with an expression such as avg_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) asserting that only a single, unsplit request is executed would have caught the regression introduced by interpolating before the split decision.

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. The newly introduced ContextualLoggerMiddleware does not add this information, resulting in missing traceID in plugin request logs and impacting debugging and request tracing capabilities.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
traceID field dropped from 'Plugin Request Completed' log line

The previous implementation of logRequest explicitly appended "traceID" to the log parameters via tracing.TraceIDFromContext(ctx, false), and the tracing import was removed along with that code. The replacement relies on m.logger.FromContext(ctx), which only picks up contextual attributes stored in the context via log.WithContextualAttributes — and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware (instrumentContext) only sets endpoint, pluginId, dsName, dsUID, and uname; it never sets traceID. Nothing else in the middleware chain injects traceID as a contextual log attribute, so the traceID field that operators previously had for correlating these plugin request logs with traces silently disappears from the "Plugin Request Completed" log line whenever plugin_log_backend_requests is enabled. If traceID was intended to be kept, it should either be re-added explicitly to logParams or included in the contextual attributes by the ContextualLoggerMiddleware.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a new instance, discarding captured logs

TestLogger.FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(), i.e. a fresh, empty TestLogger. Since LoggerMiddleware now logs through m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) instead of calling the injected logger directly, any test that passes a TestLogger and then asserts on its InfoLogs/WarnLogs fields will see zero calls — the log entry is recorded on the discarded instance, so the assertion fails (or, worse, if written to tolerate absence, silently passes). The fake should return the receiver itself (return f) so logs emitted through the FromContext path are captured on the same object the test holds.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The ContextualLoggerMiddleware methods (QueryData, CallResource, CheckHealth, CollectMetrics) panic when a nil request is received. This occurs because they directly access req.PluginContext (via the instrumentContext function) without first checking if req is nil. This is a regression, as previous middleware layers gracefully handled nil requests.

false_positives.candidate:
LoggerMiddleware still constructed with logger name 'plugin.instrumentation'

CreateMiddlewares builds the LoggerMiddleware with log.New("plugin.instrumentation"). Since the InstrumentationMiddleware no longer exists (it is now MetricsMiddleware, plus a separate ContextualLoggerMiddleware), the 'plugin.instrumentation' logger name is a stale reference to the removed type and makes log source attribution misleading — log lines emitted by the LoggerMiddleware now appear to come from an 'instrumentation' component that was deliberately renamed. A name such as 'plugin.logger' or 'plugin.client' would reflect the new structure.

Test function still named TestInstrumentationMiddleware after rename

The middleware was renamed from InstrumentationMiddleware to MetricsMiddleware and the test file was renamed accordingly, but the top-level test function is still called TestInstrumentationMiddleware. This is a leftover of the rename and makes test output/searching refer to a type that no longer exists; it should be renamed to TestMetricsMiddleware for consistency with the rest of the PR.

true_positives.golden_comment: Race condition: Multiple concurrent requests could pass the device count check simultaneously and create devices beyond the limit. Consider using a database transaction or lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert limit check is racy and can exceed the configured device limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by calling CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, running the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT upsert. These are two separate statements with no transaction or locking, so N concurrent requests with distinct new device IDs can all observe count < limit and all insert, pushing the device table past deviceLimit. Since anonymous requests are unauthenticated and arrive concurrently (and each device is only cached locally per instance for 29 minutes, so multi-instance deployments re-check often), overshooting the limit under load is realistic. If the limit is meant as a hard cap, enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g., conditional insert in a transaction or a database-level constraint).

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the DB write, so the device limit is only enforced once per device

In tagDeviceUI, the cache key is set with `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` (line 87) before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, but the cache entry was already written and stays valid for ~29 minutes. On the next request from the same device, tagDeviceUI hits the cache at line 83-84 and returns nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate (client.go) no longer sees ErrDeviceLimitReached and the request is allowed. Result: a new device over the limit is rejected exactly once, then gets full anonymous access for the rest of the cache window (and the window renews each time the device is re-tagged after expiry fails again). This effectively defeats the configurable device limit this PR adds. The cache entry should only be set after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice can report ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device on MySQL

updateDevice treats `rowsAffected == 0` as 'device does not exist / not in window' and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL (grafana's DSN does not set clientFoundRows), RowsAffected counts rows actually changed, not rows matched. The UPDATE sets updated_at to the current time, but anon_device.updated_at has second precision on MySQL, so two tag refreshes for the same device within the same second with unchanged client_ip/user_agent produce no changed columns and rowsAffected == 0. An existing, in-window device then gets ErrDeviceLimitReached and its anonymous authentication fails even though it is already counted against the limit. Compare using a matched-rows semantic or restructure the check (e.g., SELECT the device first, or use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS).

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
New device_limit option is not documented in the config files

The PR adds `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` under [auth.anonymous], but the changed-files list does not include conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini, so the new `device_limit` option is undocumented and invisible to administrators browsing or generating config. Per Grafana convention, new ini options should be added (commented, with description) to conf/defaults.ini and conf/sample.ini; otherwise the feature is undiscoverable.

No test that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a *new* device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached once the limit is reached. The other half of the feature — that a device already present in anon_device (and within the 30-day window) is still allowed via the updateDevice path when count >= deviceLimit — is untested. A regression that rejects existing devices at the limit (e.g., the MySQL rowsAffected issue, or a broken WHERE clause in updateDevice) would not be caught. Add a case: limit=1, create device A, then call CreateOrUpdateDevice again for device A and assert it succeeds and updates the row.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Routine cleanup progress logged at Error level, including full ID lists

The new cleanup paths in CleanAnnotations and CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags emit `r.log.Error(...)` for normal, successful progress (e.g. line 534 "Annotations to clean by time", plus lines 537, 554, 557, 576, 579). These are not errors; they fire on every cleanup batch, and each message includes the full `ids` slice and the raw SQL condition. With the default batch size (and especially with the new 1-minute cleanup cadence in cleanup.go), this will flood error-level logs and any error-based alerting/monitoring with noise, and with large configured batch sizes (e.g. 32767) each line logs tens of thousands of IDs. These should be Debug level and should not dump the full ID list (a count suffices).

true_positives.golden_comment: The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Cleanup ticker changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs

The diff changes the CleanUpService ticker from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This service runs many jobs besides annotation cleanup: deleting expired snapshots, dashboard versions, expired images, user invites, stale short URLs, and stale query history, plus a filesystem scan of temp directories. All of these now run 10x more frequently, which increases database and filesystem load across every Grafana instance, and the change is not mentioned in the PR description (which is scoped to the annotation deadlock fix). Since the annotation cleanup itself is already batched and self-paced, this global cadence change does not appear necessary for the fix and should either be reverted or justified and called out explicitly.

false_positives.candidate:
Placeholder-limit workaround only applied to SQLite, not MySQL/Postgres

deleteByIDs special-cases SQLite's 999-parameter limit by inlining IDs into the DELETE statement, but for other dialects it always emits `len(ids)` placeholders. MySQL and Postgres both cap parameters at 65535 per statement; AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize is operator-configurable, so setting it above 65535 on MySQL/Postgres makes the DELETE fail every cycle (cleanup silently broken until the config is fixed and the error noticed). Since the code already handles the same class of problem for SQLite, the limit check should be applied per dialect (or the batch size validated at startup) rather than only for SQLite.

true_positives.golden_comment: The context is being created with d.Log instead of the log variable that was initialized with additional context values (name, kind, method). This means those values won't be propagated to the logging context.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete installs the base logger into the context instead of the enriched one

Delete builds log := d.Log.WithValues("name", name, "kind", options.Kind, "method", method) but then calls klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log), dropping all of those values. Every other method in this file installs its enriched logger. Downstream log lines emitted via klog.FromContext during a delete will lack the name/kind/method fields.

true_positives.golden_comment: Inconsistency: using name instead of options.Kind for metrics recording differs from other methods.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Delete records storage duration with the object name as the resource label

On the success path of Delete, d.recordStorageDuration(false, mode3Str, name, method, startStorage) passes the object name where every other call site passes options.Kind as the resource label. This both mislabels the metric (deletes appear under a different 'resource' than all other operations) and turns a bounded label (kind) into an unbounded one (every individual object name becomes a label value), causing a Prometheus cardinality explosion on servers with many objects.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the HTTP handler returns

In Create (and identically in Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) the fire-and-forget goroutine does context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...) on the incoming request ctx. The request context is cancelled as soon as the API handler finishes writing the response, which typically happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write returns — long before the 10s timeout matters. The legacy write will therefore be aborted with context.Canceled in the common case (any legacy call slower than handler teardown), so the 'safe measure' legacy copy silently diverges from unified storage, with the failure only visible as a metric bump. The goroutine should derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or a detached background context carrying the logger/values) so the legacy write can actually complete.

Create storage-error path records a legacy-duration metric

When d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) even though no legacy call was ever made and the measured duration is the unified-storage create. It should be recordStorageDuration(true, ...). As written, unified-storage create failures are reported as legacy errors and the storage error metric is never incremented, making alerting on unified-storage failures blind to create errors.

Delete no longer attempts legacy deletion when unified storage returns NotFound

The previous implementation distinguished NotFound: if d.Storage.Delete returned an IsNotFound error it still went on to delete from Legacy, so objects that exist only in the legacy store (e.g., written before mode 3 was enabled, or whose legacy write succeeded while unified failed) could still be cleaned up. The new code returns immediately on any error from unified storage, so a Get in mode 3 would 404 while the object still exists in the legacy store, and there is no way through the dual writer to delete that orphaned legacy object. This leaves permanent legacy orphans during the migration window mode 3 is designed for.

DeleteCollection legacy write records a storage-duration metric

Inside the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy delete-collection latency and failures are attributed to unified storage, and the legacy metric for this method is never populated.

Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order

Because every mutating operation spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write with no sequencing, two rapid operations on the same object (e.g., Update then Delete, or two Updates) can be applied to the legacy store in the opposite order — the delete goroutine can run before the update goroutine, resurrecting the object in legacy, or an older update can overwrite a newer one. Since mode 3 treats legacy as the fallback store to migrate back to, this reordering can leave the legacy copy in a state that never matched unified storage. Some ordering mechanism (per-key queue, or at minimum synchronous ordering guarantees) is needed.

Legacy Update re-derives the object from legacy's own old object instead of mirroring what unified storage stored

The previous mode 3 Update fetched the old object, computed the updated object once via objInfo.UpdatedObject, and used updateWrapper so that the legacy store persisted exactly the object returned by unified storage. The new code hands the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update inside the goroutine, so legacy's store invokes objInfo.UpdatedObject against legacy's own (possibly stale) old object. If legacy is behind unified storage (which is expected in mode 3, since legacy writes are async), the legacy update can conflict or produce a different object than what unified storage stored, and the resulting error is only counted in a metric — never logged and never surfaced. The legacy 'safety net' copy can thus silently and permanently drift from unified storage.

Mode 3 integration tests assert legacy API state synchronously while legacy writes are asynchronous

doPlaylistTests contains checks like 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' that write through the k8s API and immediately read via the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a detached goroutine after the response is returned, so these assertions race with the legacy write: on a loaded CI worker the legacy GET can observe the pre-write state and fail intermittently (and combined with the request-context cancellation in dualwriter_mode3.go, the legacy write may never land at all). The mode 3 subtests need to poll/wait for the legacy state to converge instead of asserting it immediately.

Update storage-error path records a legacy-duration metric

When d.Storage.Update fails, d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) is called even though the failure came from unified storage and no legacy update was attempted. It should be recordStorageDuration(true, ...). Unified-storage update failures will be misattributed to legacy in the dual-writer metrics.

true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes duplicate expensive loads

GetWebAssets uses a read-then-write lock pattern, but after releasing the read lock and acquiring the write lock (line 48), it never re-checks whether another goroutine populated entryPointAssetsCache in the gap. On a cold cache in non-dev mode, N concurrent requests will all pass the initial nil check, then serialize on the write lock and each re-execute the full load (parsing assets-manifest.json, calling cfg.GetContentDeliveryURL, and potentially an HTTP fetch from the CDN once the hardcoded cdn variable is enabled). Only the last result is kept, so the earlier loads are wasted work, and different concurrent callers can receive different *EntryPointAssets instances despite the cache semantics. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

false_positives.candidate:
No regression test exercising concurrent GetWebAssets calls

This PR fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache variable, but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently (e.g., from multiple goroutines with the race detector enabled via `go test -race`). Without such a test, a future refactor that drops or weakens the mutex guarding would not be caught by CI, and the race this PR fixes would silently regress. A simple test spinning up several goroutines calling GetWebAssets against a temp manifest file in both Dev and non-Dev environments would cover the guarded paths.

true_positives.golden_comment: The enableSqlExpressions function has flawed logic that always returns false, effectively disabling SQL expressions unconditionally:
true_positives.matched_candidate:
enableSqlExpressions always returns false via convoluted dead logic with no explanation

The new helper `enableSqlExpressions` computes `enabled := !h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(featuremgmt.FlagSqlExpressions)` and then returns false on every branch — the variable and the `if` are dead code and the function always returns false. That is presumably the intent (hard-disable SQL expressions for the CVE-2024-9264 fix), but nothing in the code says so. The double negative reads like a bug, and a future maintainer may 'fix' it to `return h.features.IsEnabledGlobally(...)`, silently re-enabling the SQL/DuckDB execution path that was disabled for security reasons. The function should be a plain `return false` with a comment stating the feature is intentionally disabled, or the flag should be checked with an explicit blocklist comment.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The DB methods NewInMemoryDB().RunCommands, DB.QueryFramesInto, and DB.TablesList in pkg/expr/sql/db.go return hardcoded 'not implemented' errors after removing the go-duck dependency.

false_positives.candidate:
Legacy UnmarshalSQLCommand path is only blocked implicitly by the stubbed DB erroring out

The explicit disable check was added only in ExpressionQueryReader.ReadQuery (pkg/expr/reader.go). The legacy parsing path, UnmarshalSQLCommand, has no feature-flag or disabled check; SQL execution through it is prevented only because NewSQLCommand calls sql.TablesList, which now fails because the stubbed DB.RunCommands returns 'not implemented'. If the stub in pkg/expr/sql/db.go is later replaced with a real implementation (the file keeps the full go-duck API surface, suggesting it is meant to be swapped back), the legacy path would execute SQL with no gate at all. An explicit rejection (mirroring the reader.go check, or an error in NewSQLCommand itself) should guard this path so the security fix does not depend on an incidental error from a stub.

No regression test verifies SQL expressions are rejected after the security fix

This PR disables SQL expressions to remediate an RCE/LFI vulnerability (CVE-2024-9264), but adds no test asserting the new behavior: e.g. that ReadQuery returns an error for QueryTypeSQL even when the sqlExpressions feature flag is enabled, and that NewSQLCommand/sql.TablesList fail. Without such a test, a future change that restores the go-duck dependency or 'fixes' the always-false enableSqlExpressions helper would re-open the vulnerability without any CI signal.

User-facing error says 'sqlExpressions is not implemented' although the feature exists but is deliberately disabled

When a user submits an SQL expression query, ReadQuery now rejects it with the error `sqlExpressions is not implemented`. This is misleading: the feature is implemented but has been disabled for security reasons (CVE-2024-9264). Users who had the sqlExpressions feature flag enabled will see a message implying their Grafana build lacks the feature rather than that it was turned off, which will generate confusing support tickets. The message should state that SQL expressions are disabled/unavailable.

true_positives.golden_comment: A race condition in BuildIndex allows multiple goroutines to concurrently build the same expensive index for the same key. This is caused by moving the b.cacheMu lock from protecting the entire function to only protecting the final cache assignment.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Removing the function-wide lock in BuildIndex allows concurrent builds of the same index

Previously BuildIndex held b.cacheMu for its entire duration, serializing all index builds. The PR removes that lock and only locks around the final cache write, but there is no per-key serialization anywhere else: searchSupport.getOrCreateIndex (pkg/storage/unified/resource/search.go) does GetIndex-then-build with no guard (its own TODO admits this), so two concurrent Search calls, or a Search concurrent with a watch event, for the same NamespacedResource can both enter BuildIndex. Consequences: (1) for file-backed indexes (size > FileThreshold), both goroutines call bleve.New on the same directory path, which will fail with a lock/already-exists error or risk on-disk corruption, surfacing as spurious request errors; (2) both goroutines write b.cache[key], so the loser's fully built index is overwritten without ever being closed, leaking file handles and memory. The speedup is real for distinct keys, but same-key builds need a singleflight/per-key mutex to stay safe.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling s.search.TotalDocs() here may race with concurrent index creation: TotalDocs iterates b.cache without synchronization, and the event watcher goroutine started just above could trigger BuildIndex writes concurrently, potentially causing a concurrent map read/write panic.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TotalDocs iterates the index cache map without holding cacheMu

bleveBackend.TotalDocs ranges over b.cache with no lock, while BuildIndex now writes to that map under a short-lived cacheMu critical section. The PR adds a new caller: searchSupport.init logs s.search.TotalDocs() (search.go line 216) immediately after starting the watch goroutine, and that goroutine can concurrently call getOrCreateIndex -> BuildIndex -> `b.cache[key] = idx` when an event arrives for a namespace that was below the initMinSize threshold and thus not pre-built. A concurrent map read and write is a fatal runtime error in Go (not a recoverable panic), so this can crash the server during or right after startup. TotalDocs should take cacheMu.RLock() before iterating.

false_positives.candidate:
Data races on shared err and totalBatchesIndexed in concurrent init goroutines

In searchSupport.init, each errgroup goroutine does `totalBatchesIndexed++` and `_, _, err = s.build(...)`, where both variables are shared outer-scope variables also accessed by the main goroutine (err is reassigned by `err = group.Wait()`, totalBatchesIndexed is read for the span event). With initWorkers > 1 — which this PR explicitly promotes by moving init to startup and speeding up concurrent builds — these are genuine data races that `go test -race` will flag, and the err returned by an individual goroutine may be overwritten by a sibling goroutine's build result. Each goroutine should use a local err and the counter should be an atomic (or dropped).

Storage-server integration test is now skipped entirely on postgres

The PR adds a skip for GRAFANA_TEST_DB=postgres in TestIntegrationWillRunInstrumentationServerWhenTargetHasNoHttpServer, so CI no longer exercises the storage-server module target (which is exactly the startup path this PR changes by moving unified-storage init into server construction) against postgres. The TODO acknowledges it only fails in Drone, but merging this means the postgres variant can silently rot; consider skipping only in CI (e.g., detecting the Drone environment) or fixing the underlying issue before relying on this test to validate the new eager init behavior.

Watch goroutine panics on nil event when the events channel closes at shutdown

The goroutine started at the end of searchSupport.init does `v := <-events` in a loop without checking the ok flag. The SQL backend's poller closes the stream channel when the backend is stopped (defer close(stream) in backend.poller), at which point this receive returns nil forever and s.handleEvent(watchctx, nil) immediately dereferences evt.Type, panicking the process. Because this PR moves init from the first gRPC call to server construction, this goroutine now always runs whenever search is configured, so every shutdown of a search-enabled server (including the integration test in this PR that calls ms.Shutdown) risks a process-crashing panic. The receive should be `v, ok := <-events; if !ok { return }`.

true_positives.golden_comment: Cleanup reference uses incorrect alias - should be 'idp-alias-' + i instead of 'alias'.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Test cleanup registers removal of literal alias "alias" instead of the created IDP aliases

In the new testCacheIDPForLogin, the cleanup is registered as getCleanup().addCleanup(testRealm().identityProviders().get("alias")::remove) (lines 381 and 425; the same copy-paste bug exists in the pre-existing testCacheIDPByOrg at line 303). The literal string "alias" is used instead of the actual alias variable (e.g. "idp-alias-" + i). As a result the 21 identity providers created by this test (idp-alias-0 … idp-alias-20) are never removed, while teardown attempts to delete a non-existent IDP with alias "alias". The leaked, mostly enabled IDPs persist in the shared "test" realm and can pollute subsequent tests in the class and other test classes that count or render identity providers for that realm. The cleanup should reference the created alias, e.g. final String alias = "idp-alias-" + i; getCleanup().addCleanup(() -> testRealm().identityProviders().get(alias).remove()).

false_negatives.golden_comment: InfinispanIdentityProviderStorageProvider.getForLogin() recursively calls session.identityProviders().getById() instead of idpDelegate.getById(), causing the cache lookup to re-enter the same caching layer.

false_positives.candidate:
update() compares against the organization-aware wrapped model, causing missed login-cache invalidations when the IDP's organization is disabled

In update(), the 'original' model used by registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate is obtained via getById(), which returns the model wrapped by createOrganizationAwareIdentityProviderModel. That wrapper overrides isEnabled() to also require the linked organization to be enabled. getLoginPredicate() (LoginFilter.ENABLED) calls isEnabled(), so when an IDP's organization is currently disabled, predicate(original) evaluates to false even though the IDP itself is a valid login IDP. Now consider this sequence: (1) an org-linked public IDP is in the cached getForLogin(ORG_ONLY/ALL) ID list; (2) the organization is disabled; (3) the admin updates the IDP to make it unavailable for login — sets hideOnLogin=true, linkOnly=true, or broker_public=false — while keeping it enabled. predicate(updated) is false, and because predicate(original) is also false (due to the disabled org, not the IDP), registerIDPLoginInvalidationOnUpdate hits the first 'both false' branch and registers NO invalidation of the .idp.login.* caches. The IDP's internal id therefore stays in the cached login ID sets. (4) When the organization is re-enabled (which does not invalidate the login caches, by design), getForLogin serves the stale cached id, getById returns a wrapper whose isEnabled() is now true, and OrganizationAwareIdentityProviderBean only re-checks isEnabled() — it does not re-check hideOnLogin, linkOnly, or BROKER_PUBLIC in the ORG_ONLY/ALL paths — so a broker the admin explicitly hid or made private is displayed and usable on the login pages. The fix is to compute the original login-eligibility from the raw delegate model (or an unwrapped copy) rather than from the organization-aware wrapper, so org enablement does not poison the comparison.

true_positives.golden_comment: Returns wrong provider (default keystore instead of BouncyCastle)
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getBouncyCastleProvider() returns the JVM default keystore provider, not a BouncyCastle provider

`AuthzClientCryptoProvider.getBouncyCastleProvider()` is implemented as `KeyStore.getInstance(KeyStore.getDefaultType()).getProvider()`, which returns whatever JCA provider backs the default keystore (typically the SUN provider) — not a BouncyCastle provider as the interface contract (`@return BouncyCastle security provider. Can be either non-FIPS or FIPS based provider`) documents. Any caller that obtains this provider and then requests BouncyCastle-specific algorithms or keystores (e.g. BCFKS, PKCS7Padding via BC) from it will fail at runtime, and callers that use a non-null return value as a signal that BouncyCastle is available will be misled. WildFlyElytronProvider demonstrates that returning null is an accepted implementation; if the authz-client genuinely has no BouncyCastle, this should return null (or the contract/hack should be documented) rather than returning an unrelated provider.

true_positives.golden_comment: Abstract order() method on CryptoProvider may break backward compatibility with existing implementations
true_positives.matched_candidate:
New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations

The PR adds a new abstract method `int order()` to the public `CryptoProvider` interface in keycloak-common. Any third-party or downstream CryptoProvider implementation compiled against a previous keycloak-common version does not implement this method. With the new `CryptoIntegration.detectProvider` code, `Comparator.comparingInt(CryptoProvider::order)` invokes `order()` on every provider found by the ServiceLoader, so an older compiled provider will throw `AbstractMethodError` during `CryptoIntegration.init`, completely failing startup instead of just being sorted differently. Making it a default method (e.g. `default int order() { return 0; }`) would preserve binary/source compatibility for existing implementations.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Dead code exists where ASN1Encoder instances are created and written to, but their results are immediately discarded. The actual encoding is performed by new ASN1Encoder instances created in the subsequent return statement, rendering the earlier operations useless.
When length starts at -1 from indefinite-length encoding, the arithmetic 'length = length - bytes.length' will behave unexpectedly, potentially leading to incorrect processing of encoded data.

false_positives.candidate:
ECDSA conversion test only round-trips through the same implementation, so it cannot catch standard-noncompliant DER encoding

The new test verifies `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` by feeding the output of `concatenatedRSToASN1DER` back into `asn1derToConcatenatedRS` and asserting equality. Because both directions are implemented by the same new ASN1Encoder/ASN1Decoder code, any self-consistent but incorrect encoding still passes — for example, if both the encoder and decoder used a wrong tag constant for INTEGER or SEQUENCE, or mis-encoded lengths, the round-trip assertion would still succeed while real Keycloak servers would reject the produced JWS signatures. The primary purpose of this PR is producing standard DER signatures for ES256/ES384/ES512 client authentication without BouncyCastle, so the test should additionally verify the DER output against an independent implementation (e.g. `Signature.verify` with the JCA Signature, or fixed known-answer test vectors comparing against BouncyCastle's encoding), and ideally cover the end-to-end AuthzClient-with-ES256-credentials path.

Multiple real providers with equal order() are now silently resolved by classpath order instead of failing fast

Previously, `detectProvider` threw an IllegalStateException when more than one CryptoProvider was on the classpath, which caught misconfigured deployments. Now providers are sorted by `order()` descending and the first is silently used, with the rest only logged at debug level. However all three 'real' providers (DefaultCryptoProvider, WildFlyElytronProvider, FIPS1402Provider) return the same order value 200, so if two of their jars end up on the classpath together, the winner is decided by ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order — non-obvious and environment-dependent. This is especially risky for FIPS: if both crypto/default and crypto/fips1402 jars are present, the non-FIPS provider may silently be selected (and even when FIPS wins, merely instantiating DefaultCryptoProvider during ServiceLoader iteration registers the non-FIPS BouncyCastle provider in the JVM security provider list as a constructor side effect). Equal-order ties among full providers should still be treated as a configuration error rather than silently picked.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getClientsWithPermission(String scope), iterating resourceStore.findByType(server, AdminPermissionsSchema.CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) and returning resource.getName() will only ever consider the type-level 'Clients' resource (per-client resources have no type) and return its name, while AvailableRoleMappingResource#getRoleIdsWithPermissions expects actual client IDs to pass to realm.getClientById, which can lead to incorrect behavior or a null client and subsequent failures.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getClientsWithPermission can never return real client IDs

getClientsWithPermission(scope) iterates resourceStore.findByType(server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE, ...) and adds resource.getName() to the result. However, per-client resources are created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource via resourceStore.create(resourceServer, name, owner) which never sets the resource type — only the type-level "Clients" resource created in init() has type set. So findByType never matches per-client resources (their type is null), meaning clients the caller was explicitly granted per-client permissions on are never returned. The only possible match is the "Clients" type resource itself, whose name is the literal string "Clients" — not a client ID — so the returned set is either empty or contains a bogus entry that callers comparing against client IDs (e.g., client listing filters) cannot use. The method effectively never returns a valid client ID.

true_positives.golden_comment: In ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission, the method getResourceTypeResource could return null, leading to a NullPointerException in findByResource. Defensive null checks are needed to prevent this issue.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
hasPermission(ClientModel, String) may call findByResource with a null resource

In the fallback branch, resource = AdminPermissionsSchema.SCHEMA.getResourceTypeResource(session, server, CLIENTS_RESOURCE_TYPE) can return null (e.g., when the "Clients" type resource doesn't exist, or supportsAuthorizationSchema is false). The very next statement calls authz.getStoreFactory().getPolicyStore().findByResource(server, resource) without a null check, which can throw a NullPointerException in store implementations that dereference the resource (e.g., resource.getId()) instead of simply denying access. A null check returning false should guard this call.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Remove unused getEvaluationContext private method in ClientPermissionsV2 - it is defined but never called

Inconsistent feature flag bug causing orphaned permissions. The AdminPermissions event listener, responsible for cleaning up permissions upon role, client, or group removal, is incorrectly guarded by the ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ (V1) feature flag. This is inconsistent with other methods in the class that use ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2. Consequently, if ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled but V1 is not, the permission cleanup logic will not execute, leading to orphaned permission data. Cleanup should occur regardless of which fine-grained authorization version is enabled.

In hasPermission(ClientModel client, String scope), the resource lookup uses findByName(server, client.getId(), server.getId()), but AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource creates per-client resources with the owner set to resourceServer.getClientId(), so this lookup will never find those resources and will always fall back to the 'all-clients' resource, effectively ignoring client-specific permissions.

false_positives.candidate:
Javadoc on requireView()/requireViewClientScopes() describes a boolean return for void methods

The new javadoc for requireView() says "Returns true if canView() returns true" and requireViewClientScopes() says "Returns true if canViewClientScopes() returns true". Both methods are void and their contract is to throw ForbiddenException when the corresponding can* check fails (as correctly documented on the other require* methods). The documentation is misleading about the method contract and should say it throws ForbiddenException if the check returns false.

No migration for realms whose admin-permissions resource server was initialized with the Users-only schema

init() returns early when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null, so realms that enabled FGAP V2 before this change keep a resource server containing only the Users resource and the Users scopes. The new Clients scopes (configure, map-roles-client-scope, map-roles-composite) and the "Clients" type resource are never created for them. Consequences after upgrade: creating a Clients scope-permission fails validation in getScope with ModelValidationException("Scope [configure] does not exist."); creating a client resource in getOrCreateResource throws ModelException("No scopes found.") because the new scopes can't be found; and ClientPermissionsV2.hasPermission falls back to a null "Clients" resource. An upgrade/re-initialization path that adds the new scopes and the Clients type resource to existing admin-permissions resource servers is needed.

canExchangeTo throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking token exchange whenever V2 feature is on

canExchangeTo(ClientModel, ClientModel, AccessToken) throws UnsupportedOperationException. The standard token exchange flow (AbstractTokenExchangeProvider) builds an evaluator via AdminPermissions.evaluator(session, realm, auth) and calls auth.clients().canExchangeTo(authenticatedClient, targetClient, token) for every client-to-client exchange, regardless of whether the realm uses fine-grained admin permissions. With ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 enabled, MgmtPermissionsV2.clients() returns this class, so any token exchange to a different target client results in an unhandled UnsupportedOperationException (HTTP 500) instead of an allow/deny decision. The unused getEvaluationContext helper and unused TOKEN_EXCHANGE import suggest this method was left unfinished; at minimum it should fail closed with a proper denial rather than throwing.

canMapRoles/canMapCompositeRoles/canMapClientScopeRoles lack the manage fallback, denying role-based and manage-permission admins

The three canMap* overrides only check hasPermission(client, MAP_ROLES / MAP_ROLES_COMPOSITE / MAP_ROLES_CLIENT_SCOPE). In V1 (ClientPermissions) these methods short-circuit with a manage check (manage-clients admin role / manage permission on the client), and the V2 Users implementation follows the same rule — testTransitiveUserPermissions in this PR asserts that a manage permission on users implies map-roles. Here, an administrator holding the manage-clients realm role or an FGAP manage permission on a client (or on all clients) gets canManage(client) == true but canMapRoles(client) == false, so role mapping for that client is denied. This is an access-control regression versus V1 and is inconsistent with the Users V2 semantics; the tests only pass because they grant the map-roles scopes explicitly.

getResourceName does not handle the Clients resource type, returning null display names

getResourceName(session, policy, resource) only special-cases USERS resourceType (mapping to "All users" or the username). For a policy with resourceType "Clients" it falls through to resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set for resources created via getOrCreateResource or init(), so the admin console/REST representation of client permissions shows blank resource names. It should mirror the Users handling (e.g., "All clients" for the type resource and the client's clientId for per-client resources).

setPermissionsEnabled throws UnsupportedOperationException, breaking client deletion when FGAP V2 is enabled

ClientPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled(ClientModel, boolean) unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). However, AdminPermissions.registerListener (AdminPermissions.java, in the ClientRemovedEvent branch) calls management(session, realm).clients().setPermissionsEnabled(cast.getClient(), false) on every client removal. When Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ_V2 is enabled, AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2 and clients() now returns this ClientPermissionsV2, so deleting any client fires the event and the listener throws. Provider event listeners run synchronously inside the transaction, so the exception propagates and rolls back client deletion entirely. The V2 variant should either no-op here (V2 cleans up via orphan-resource removal) or the listener should skip clients for V2.

true_positives.golden_comment: Need to add changelog/release notes documenting the exit code change and migration guidance
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Recreate-upgrade exit code changed from 4 to 3, breaking the documented scripting contract

The previous release documented and implemented exit code 4 as 'Rolling Upgrade is not possible, shut down the deployment before applying the new configuration' (RECREATE_UPGRADE_EXIT_CODE = 4). This PR reassigns 4 to FEATURE_DISABLED and changes the recreate signal to 3. The update-compatibility guide explicitly tells users not to rely on anything except the command's exit code, so existing CI/CD pipelines written against the old contract (e.g., 'if exit code == 4 then do a recreate upgrade') will silently misbehave after upgrade: a recreate-required check now returns 3 (which such scripts will treat as an unknown/error case, potentially aborting the pipeline or worse, proceeding as if rolling were possible depending on the fallback), and a disabled feature now returns 4 (which such scripts will interpret as 'recreate required'). If this renumbering is intentional, it needs an explicit callout in the release notes/upgrading guide so users can update their automation, not just a silent change in the command's own doc page.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Incorrect method call for exit codes. The picocli.exit() method calls System.exit() directly, which is problematic:

false_positives.candidate:
No test asserts the exit codes that the documentation declares as the stable contract

The docs added in this PR (update-compatibility.adoc) present the exit code table (0 = rolling possible, 3 = recreate required, 4 = feature disabled) as the supported scripting interface, yet the tests only assert on log output. In particular, testFeatureNotEnabled asserts only the stderr message but never checks that the process actually exits with CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED (4), and testWrongVersions asserts the error text but never checks exit code 3. If picocli.exit(...) were skipped, mis-mapped, or a PropertyException (exit code 2) were thrown instead, all tests would still pass while the documented contract would be broken. Add assertions like assertEquals(CompatibilityResult.FEATURE_DISABLED, result.exitCode()) and assertEquals(3, ...) for the recreate case.

true_positives.golden_comment: In GroupPermissionsV2.canManage(), the permission fallback checks for both VIEW and MANAGE scopes (hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE)), but canManage() should only grant access for MANAGE scope, not VIEW. This means users with only VIEW permission on groups can pass the canManage() check, granting them write access they should not have. The canView() method correctly checks both VIEW and MANAGE, but canManage() should only check MANAGE.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
canManage() is satisfied by the view scope, allowing group management with view-only permission

GroupPermissionsV2.canManage() returns hasPermission(null, AdminPermissionsSchema.VIEW, AdminPermissionsSchema.MANAGE), i.e. an admin holding only the view scope on the Groups resource type is treated as able to manage groups globally. The no-arg requireManage() guards privileged operations — for example GroupsResource.addTopLevelGroup calls auth.groups().requireManage() — so an admin with a view-only "all groups" permission can create top-level groups (privilege escalation). The per-group overload canManage(GroupModel) correctly requires only the MANAGE scope; the no-arg variant should do the same. The javadoc added to GroupPermissionEvaluator.canManage() in this PR also documents VIEW as sufficient and should be corrected.

true_positives.golden_comment: In getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, hasPermission is called with groupResource.getId() and the same groupResource.getId() is added to granted, but hasPermission resolves resources by name (treating the argument as a group id) and the GroupPermissionEvaluator contract says this method returns group IDs that are later used as UserModel.GROUPS and in getUsersCount group filters. This mismatch means per-group VIEW_MEMBERS/MANAGE_MEMBERS permissions may not yield the expected group IDs for filtering and counts, and evaluation may effectively only look at the type-level 'all-groups' resource; consider revisiting whether this should operate on the underlying group ids (resource names) instead so it aligns with the JPA queries and the interface contract.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
getGroupIdsWithViewPermission uses the authorization resource UUID instead of the group id

In GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission, the findByType callback calls hasPermission(groupResource.getId(), ...) and granted.add(groupResource.getId()). Per-group resources are created in AdminPermissionsSchema.getOrCreateResource with the resource name set to the group id, whereas Resource.getId() is the internal UUID of the authorization resource entity. Two consequences: (1) hasPermission does resourceStore.findByName(server, groupId), so passing the resource UUID never finds the per-group resource and silently falls back to evaluating the "Groups" all-resource — per-group view-members/manage-members grants are never detected, or the wrong resource is evaluated; (2) the returned set contains resource UUIDs, but callers (UsersResource.searchForUser, UsersResource.getUsersCount, BruteForceUsersResource) store it in the UserModel.GROUPS session attribute / pass it to user-count queries that expect group ids, so user searches and counts for group-scoped admins are filtered by non-existent groups and return wrong (usually empty) results. The method should use groupResource.getName().

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting a group throws UnsupportedOperationException when FGAP V2 is enabled

AdminPermissions.registerListener registers a ProviderEventListener (registered whenever Profile.Feature.ADMIN_FINE_GRAINED_AUTHZ is enabled, which V2 implies) that on GroupModel.GroupRemovedEvent calls management(session, realm).groups().setPermissionsEnabled(group, false). With the V2 feature enabled, AdminPermissions.management() returns MgmtPermissionsV2, whose groups() method (added in this PR) returns GroupPermissionsV2, and GroupPermissionsV2.setPermissionsEnabled unconditionally throws UnsupportedOperationException("Not supported in V2"). Provider events are published synchronously during group removal, so deleting any group with V2 enabled propagates this exception, fails the DELETE request and rolls back the transaction. Before this PR, MgmtPermissionsV2 did not override groups(), so the V1 implementation handled the event without throwing. The V2 class should either implement the cleanup of the group's authorization resources/permissions or make these management methods no-ops instead of throwing on this path.

No upgrade path for realms whose admin-permissions client already exists

init() returns immediately when realm.getAdminPermissionsClient() != null, so realms where fine-grained admin permissions V2 were initialized before this change never receive the new group scopes (manage-membership, manage-members, view-members) or the "Groups" all-resource. In such realms, creating a group permission fails at runtime: getScope() throws ModelValidationException("Scope [...] does not exist.") and getOrCreateResource() throws ModelException("No scopes found."), while GroupPermissionsV2's fallback getResourceTypeResource(session, server, "Groups") returns null. A migration or schema-reconciliation step for existing resource servers is needed so upgraded realms can use the new Groups resource type.

Per-instance resources are created without a resource type

getOrCreateResource creates per-instance resources (for a specific user, group, or client) via resourceStore.create(...) and updateScopes(...) but never calls resource.setType(resourceType). Only the "all resources" created in init() get a type. GroupPermissionsV2.getGroupIdsWithViewPermission enumerates per-group resources via resourceStore.findByType(server, "Groups", ...), so those resources are never returned there, and any type-based lookup/fallback in the policy engine will not see them either. The resource type should be set (resource.setType(resourceType)) when the resource is created.

getResourceName has no handling for Groups resources

getResourceName only resolves a human-readable name for the Users resource type; for every other type it returns resource.getDisplayName(), which is never set for resources created by getOrCreateResource. For a Groups-type policy the resource name is the group id, so permission listings in the admin console will render an empty/null resource name for group permissions. A GROUPS branch should resolve the group (e.g., to its name or path), or at minimum fall back to resource.getName() instead of the unset display name.

true_positives.golden_comment: The translation is in Italian instead of Lithuanian. This should be translated to Lithuanian to match the file's locale (messages_lt.properties).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Lithuanian totpStep1 replaced with Italian text

The Lithuanian translation of `totpStep1` was changed from Lithuanian to `Installa una delle seguenti applicazioni sul tuo cellulare:`, which is Italian, not Lithuanian. Users with the Lithuanian locale will see an Italian sentence on the OTP setup page of the account console. Diff-trimming code can throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException

When a sanitized value differs from the original, the code trims common prefix (`start`) and common suffix (`end`) independently. If the common prefix and suffix overlap — i.e. start + end exceeds the length of one of the strings — then `value.substring(start, value.length() - end)` or `sanitized.substring(start, sanitized.length() - end)` is called with beginIndex > endIndex and throws StringIndexOutOfBoundsException. Use `multiprocessing.context.BaseProcess` (or `multiprocessing.process.BaseProcess`) for the isinstance check instead.

On graceful shutdown, in-flight queued work is simply abandoned (it will be redelivered since offsets are not committed, but the class docstring's 'No item is lost' guarantee and the arroyo join contract — wait up to timeout for in-flight work to finish — are not honored, and the final processed-but-uncommitted offsets are not flushed, causing avoidable duplicate processing on every restart).

The test mocks the result processor to raise on the first message and asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`. But the implementation in OrderedQueueWorker.run completes offsets in a finally block even when processing raises, so both offsets become committable and the commit loop will commit offset 102. The test only passes because the commit thread waits 1.0s before its first commit and the test finishes (including its extra time.sleep(0.2)) well before that on a fast machine; under load or with a different commit interval it becomes flaky, and worse, it encodes the exact opposite of the real behavior, masking the message-loss issue where failed items are committed.

After submitting 10 work items to a pool whose 3 worker threads are actively draining, the test immediately asserts `stats['total_items'] > 0`. If the workers process all items before get_stats() runs (likely on a fast machine since the result_processor is trivial), total_items will be 0 and the assertion fails nondeterministically. The test should block the processor (e.g. with an event) before checking queue depth, or drop the assertion.

OrderedQueueWorker.run emits a metrics.gauge('remote_subscriptions.queue_worker.queue_depth', ...) for every single processed message, and wraps every message in a sentry_sdk transaction whose name includes the worker_id (f"monitors.{identifier}.worker_{worker_id}"). On a high-throughput results topic this generates a gauge emission per message (the existing batched mode only emits per batch) and creates high-cardinality transaction names (one per worker per consumer) that won't group in Sentry Performance. Consider sampling, emitting gauges only from poll(), and removing worker_id from the transaction name.
