true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator's negative-offset branch in get_result() passes cursor.offset directly as start_offset to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is True and cursor.offset < 0.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Negative-offset slicing crashes: Django does not support negative indexing

In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code does `queryset[cursor.offset:stop]` with a negative start. The comment claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically', but Django's QuerySet explicitly raises `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` for a negative slice start. Since cursor offsets are user-controlled via the cursor query parameter (`Cursor.from_string` happily parses `0:-5:0`), any admin hitting the audit log endpoint with such a cursor and `optimized_pagination=true` gets a 500. The 'advanced feature' is broken as implemented and the comment is factually wrong.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same code: the negative-offset branch in OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result passes cursor.offset as a negative start to queryset slicing when enable_advanced_features is true. The candidate adds that Django raises an error on negative slicing, but the underlying issue is the same.

true_positives.golden_comment: OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key uses floor/ceil on a datetime key (order_by='-datetime'), causing TypeError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
OptimizedCursorPaginator cannot paginate by -datetime; every optimized request 500s

The endpoint orders by `-datetime` but uses `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key` does `int(math.floor(getattr(item, self.key)))` on the `datetime` attribute — `math.floor()` on a `datetime` raises `TypeError: must be real number, not datetime.datetime`. Even if that were fixed, `value_from_cursor` returns the raw numeric cursor value, which `build_queryset` then compares against a datetime column (`col <= %s` with a float), producing a database error. Unlike `DateTimePaginator` it has no strftime/multiplier conversion, so any request with `optimized_pagination=true` from a superuser/global-access member will return HTTP 500. The new paginator is unusable for this endpoint.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug: get_item_key applies math.floor to a datetime key when ordering by -datetime, which raises a TypeError. The extra detail it gives is consistent with the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Accessing .has_global_access on organization_context.member can raise an AttributeError when organization_context is None, particularly for non-superuser non-member users.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
organization_context.member may be None, causing AttributeError for org-token auth

`enable_advanced = request.user.is_superuser or organization_context.member.has_global_access` dereferences `organization_context.member` unconditionally for non-superusers. For requests authenticated with an organization auth token (or any non-member context), `organization_context.member` is `None`, so this raises `AttributeError` and returns 500. Previously the audit log endpoint worked for any caller passing `OrganizationAuditPermission`. The member check needs a `None` guard.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe an AttributeError from accessing .has_global_access without a None guard for non-superuser, non-member callers. The golden says organization_context is None, while the candidate says organization_context.member is None. Despite that small difference, it is the same line and the same missing guard.

false_positives.candidate:
SET→ZSET migration breaks in-flight buffered segments with WRONGTYPE errors

The script and the Python producer switch segment buffer keys from Redis SETs (`sadd`/`scard`/`sunionstore`) to sorted sets (`zadd`/`zcard`/`zunionstore`), but existing keys in Redis written by the old code are still SETs. Calling `zcard`/`zunionstore` on a SET key (and likewise `p.zadd` in `SpansBuffer.process_spans`) raises a WRONGTYPE error, which aborts the Lua script and fails the whole batch of `EVALSHA` calls. During a rolling deploy — and for up to `redis_ttl` afterwards — all traces with segments buffered by the old code will cause consumer errors and those spans will not be buffered. There is no type check or migration path (e.g., probing with `type`/`object encoding`, or a key version bump).

Hardcoded 1000-span eviction ignores max_segment_spans and silently drops spans

The new eviction `if span_count > 1000 then zpopmin(set_key, span_count - 1000)` hardcodes 1000, while `SpansBuffer` still accepts a configurable `max_segment_spans` (default 1001) that is now never used — the Python-side check that dropped oversized segments with a `segment_span_count_exceeded` metric and error log was removed from `_load_segment_data`. Consequences: (1) the configured limit is silently ignored, (2) spans are evicted silently instead of the segment being dropped with an error, so downstream consumers receive incomplete segments presented as complete, and (3) `zpopmin` evicts the lowest-scored (earliest `end_timestamp_precise`) spans, which can include the segment's root span, changing flush semantics. `max_segment_spans` should either be passed into the script or removed.

Redirect-follow limit reduced from 10000 to 1000 without rationale

The redirect-chasing loop was lowered from `for i = 0, 10000` to `for i = 0, 1000`, and the old comment documenting the consequence ('segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly') was deleted. Segment trees whose redirect chain exceeds 1000 hops will now silently stop being merged — children will stay in a separate set and be flushed as their own (incomplete) segment. If the reduction is intentional for latency, the trade-off should at least be documented; otherwise deep traces lose spans relative to the old behavior.

KeyError on payloads missing end_timestamp_precise crashes the batch

`Span(..., end_timestamp_precise=val["end_timestamp_precise"], ...)` is a new hard dictionary access. The consumer only `cast`s the decoded JSON to `SpanEvent` and performs no schema validation, so any message lacking this field (older Relay payloads, malformed messages, spillover replays) raises `KeyError`, which fails the entire batch and causes it to be reprocessed in a crash loop. Previously this field was never read. Use `val.get(...)` with a fallback (e.g., 0 or the batch timestamp) if the field is not guaranteed to be present.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In BasePaginator.get_result(), when cursor.is_prev is True, it sets start_offset = offset without clamping, allowing negative offset values to be passed to queryset slicing.

true_positives.golden_comment: In _set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling(), the check `if client_sample_rate:` treats 0.0 as falsy, so a sample_rate of 0.0 is silently skipped and never set on normalized_data.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
_set_sample_rate_from_error_sampling silently swallows invalid data and drops a 0 sample rate

The new factory helper wraps everything in bare `except Exception: pass` blocks and only sets `normalized_data['sample_rate']` when `client_sample_rate` is truthy. A malformed or non-numeric `client_sample_rate` in a test event is silently ignored (the test then runs against unsampled data, producing confusing count assertions rather than a clear failure), and an explicit rate of 0 is dropped by the truthiness check. For test infrastructure, silently ignoring invalid fixture data makes failing tests much harder to diagnose; it should raise or at least validate explicitly.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says an explicit rate of 0 is dropped by the truthiness check on client_sample_rate in the same function. This is the golden issue. The candidate also raises separate concerns about exception swallowing, but that does not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: The upsampling eligibility check passes the outer dataset instead of the actual dataset used by scoped_dataset. In paths where the query ultimately runs against discover (e.g., dashboard split) while the original dataset is metrics, upsampling may be skipped even when all projects are allowlisted.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Upsampling decision uses outer `dataset`/raw request query instead of `scoped_dataset` and the actual query string

Inside `_get_event_stats`, `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects(snuba_params, organization, dataset, request)` closes over the outer `dataset` variable and the helper reads `request.GET['query']` directly, ignoring both the `scoped_dataset` parameter and the `query` argument passed to `_get_event_stats`. In the dashboard-widget split path, `_get_event_stats` is invoked with modified queries — e.g. `(<query>) AND !event.type:transaction` for the errors split (with scoped_dataset=discover) and `(<query>) AND event.type:transaction` for the transactions split — and with a scoped_dataset that can differ from the outer dataset (e.g. discover while the outer dataset is metrics_performance). As a result the upsampling transformation is applied or skipped based on the wrong dataset and the wrong query text: the transactions-only split query can get upsampled counts (wrong numbers) and the errors-only split query can fail to get upsampled counts (undercounted). The check should use `scoped_dataset` and the `query` parameter actually being executed.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: the upsampling check uses the outer dataset instead of scoped_dataset, so upsampling is skipped in the dashboard split path when it runs against discover while the outer dataset is metrics. It also raises an additional point about the query string, but the core issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Accidentally committed git submodule ('sentry-repo') pointing at the repo's own base commit

The PR adds a file `sentry-repo` containing `Subproject commit a5d290951def84afdcc4c88d2f1f20023fc36e2a` — a gitlink (embedded submodule) referencing the base commit of this very repository. This looks like a local checkout accidentally committed as a submodule. It adds a bogus gitlink to the tree, will break or slow down `git clone --recursive` / CI checkout steps (the submodule has no .gitmodules entry), and has nothing to do with the feature. It should be removed before merging.

Substring match treats negated queries like `!event.type:error` as error-focused

`_is_error_focused_query` returns True whenever the raw query string contains the substring "event.type:error". A query that explicitly *excludes* errors, e.g. `!event.type:error` (the standard way to query non-error/transaction events in discover), also contains that substring, so it will be classified as error-focused and `count()` will be rewritten to `sum(sample_weight)` over transaction rows, where sample_weight is absent/zero — returning wrong (likely zero) counts. Similarly, a query merely mentioning the field in another context (e.g. inside a quoted message search) triggers upsampling. The check should parse the query or at least exclude negated occurrences instead of doing a raw substring search.

upsampled_count sums sample_weight with no NULL fallback, zeroing out events stored without a weight

The new `upsampled_count` SnQL function compiles to `toInt64(sum(sample_weight))` and the surrounding comments state it 'assumes sample_weight exists for all events in allowlisted projects'. That assumption does not hold: allowlisting is per-project, but error events ingested *before* the project was allowlisted (or ingested without client sampling) have no sample_weight, and stats queries routinely cover historical time ranges. For rows where sample_weight is NULL, `sum` will either ignore them or return NULL (which `toInt64` turns into 0), so `count()` on an allowlisted project will silently undercount — showing 0 or fewer errors than actually occurred — for any time bucket containing older events. The aggregate should fall back to 1 for missing weights, e.g. `sum(ifNull(sample_weight, 1))`.

upsampled_count is registered as a public function, exposing it to arbitrary user queries

Unlike the neighboring private SnQL functions (e.g. the one above it with `private=True`), `upsampled_count` is registered without `private=True`, making it usable by any user in arbitrary Discover queries and datasets. Against datasets/contexts where the `sample_weight` column does not exist (transactions, etc.) this produces Snuba query errors surfaced to users, and it exposes an internal implementation detail as part of the public query API. It should be marked private and explicitly allowed only where the upsampling transformation injects it.

invalidate_upsampling_cache is dead code; allowlist changes are stale for up to 60s with no way to invalidate, and the docstring contradicts the cache

`invalidate_upsampling_cache` is defined and documented as the mechanism to call 'when the allowlist configuration changes', but nothing in the codebase calls it, so allowlist edits always take up to 60 seconds to take effect with no escape hatch. Additionally, the docstring on `_are_all_projects_error_upsampled` claims it 'reads the allowlist configuration fresh each time ... to ensure we always have the latest configuration state', which is directly contradicted by the 60-second result cache in the only caller. Either wire the invalidation into the option-change path or fix the misleading documentation.

Top-level eligibility function and its 60s caching behavior are never tested

The unit tests exercise the private helpers (`_are_all_projects_error_upsampled`, `_is_error_focused_query`, `_should_apply_sample_weight_transform`) but never call the public entry point `is_errors_query_for_error_upsampled_projects`. That function contains the PR's riskiest new logic — the cache key construction, the cache-hit short-circuit, and the combination of cached eligibility with the per-request dataset check — so regressions there (e.g. caching False forever, key collisions across project sets, ignoring the dataset check on cache hits) would not be caught by these tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Using Python’s built-in hash() to build cache keys is non-deterministic across processes (hash randomization), so keys won’t match across workers and invalidate_upsampling_cache may fail to delete them. Use a deterministic serialization of project_ids for the cache key.

true_positives.golden_comment: The test comment says the cached permissions 'allow access', but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission will still treat this scope as not allowed.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Denial-precedence test uses a non-allowing cache entry, so it doesn't prove what its comment claims

In TestService_CacheCheck/"Should deny on explicit cache deny entry", the comment says "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked", but the perm cache is seeded with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}. Because checkPermission tests the truthiness of scopeMap[scope], a false value does not grant access, so this test would pass even if the denial cache were checked after the permission cache, or if the permission cache were consulted and simply found nothing allowing. To actually pin down the precedence behavior (denial cache wins over an allowing perm cache entry), the cached value must be true — which would currently fail and exposes the stale-denial-overrides-fresh-allow problem in Check.
true_positives.reasoning: Both point to the same problem: the test comment says the cached permission allows access, but the map stores false for dashboards:uid:dash1, so checkPermission treats the scope as not allowed. The test therefore doesn't show what its comment claims.

false_positives.candidate:
Stale denial-cache entries take precedence over fresher positive permission data

In Check, the permission denial cache is consulted before the positive permission cache, and denial entries are never invalidated when the permission cache is refreshed. Sequence: (1) Check(user, dashboards:read, dash1) misses the perm cache, the DB requery denies, and a denial entry is cached (30s TTL). (2) The user is then granted read on dash1. (3) Any other Check for this user+action that falls through to the DB (e.g. for dash2) refreshes permCache via getUserPermissions with fresh data that now includes dash1. (4) A retry of Check(user, dashboards:read, dash1) hits the stale denial entry at line 117 and returns denied, even though the server's own freshly cached permission set says allow. The denial check should run after the positive cache check (allow on cached hit, then denial cache, then DB fallback), or denial entries for the user+action should be dropped when permCache is rewritten. As written, users can be denied access to just-granted resources for up to the full 30s TTL even when the server already holds fresh permissions proving the grant — which partially defeats the stated purpose of this PR (immediately accessing newly granted/created resources).

permissionCacheUsage metric recorded as a miss on a permission-cache hit that didn't grant access

When getCachedIdentityPermissions returns a cached permission set but checkPermission does not allow the request (triggering the intended DB requery fallback), execution reaches line 137 and increments permissionCacheUsage with label "false" (miss), even though the permission cache was hit. Before this change the metric was incremented inside getUserPermissions/getAnonymousPermissions strictly according to cache hit/miss, so dashboards and alerts built on the hit ratio will now show a drop in hit rate that does not reflect actual cache effectiveness. true_positives.golden_comment: The GetWebAssets function implements an incomplete double-checked locking pattern for caching web assets. The function first checks if the cache is populated using a read lock (RLock), and if the cache is empty, it acquires a write lock to populate it. However, it fails to re-check whether the cache was populated by another goroutine while waiting to acquire the write lock.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Missing re-check of cache after acquiring write lock causes duplicate expensive loads

GetWebAssets uses a read-then-write lock pattern, but after releasing the read lock and acquiring the write lock (line 48), it never re-checks whether another goroutine populated entryPointAssetsCache in the gap. On a cold cache in non-dev mode, N concurrent requests will all pass the initial nil check, then serialize on the write lock and each re-execute the full load (parsing assets-manifest.json, calling cfg.GetContentDeliveryURL, and potentially an HTTP fetch from the CDN once the hardcoded cdn variable is enabled). Only the last result is kept, so the earlier loads are wasted work, and different concurrent callers can receive different *EntryPointAssets instances despite the cache semantics. The standard fix is to re-check `if cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil { return entryPointAssetsCache, nil }` immediately after acquiring the write lock.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same flaw: GetWebAssets drops the read lock, takes the write lock, and never re-checks whether another goroutine already filled the cache. That is the incomplete double-checked locking the golden comment names.

false_positives.candidate:

This PR fixes a data race on the package-level entryPointAssetsCache variable, but adds no test that calls GetWebAssets concurrently (e.g., from multiple goroutines with the race detector enabled via `go test -race`). Without such a test, a future refactor that drops or weakens the mutex guarding would not be caught by CI, and the race this PR fixes would silently regress. A simple test spinning up several goroutines calling GetWebAssets against a temp manifest file in both Dev and non-Dev environments would cover the guarded paths.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In addition to the missing double-check, the function has a critical flaw in its error handling: it unconditionally assigns the fetch result to the cache (line 69: entryPointAssetsCache = result) regardless of whether the fetch succeeded or failed. When an error occurs during asset fetching, result is nil, and this nil value overwrites any previously valid cache entry.

This both mislabels the metric (deletes appear under a different 'resource' than all other operations) and turns a bounded label (kind) into an unbounded one (every individual object name becomes a label value), causing a Prometheus cardinality explosion on servers with many objects.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem: the metrics recording call passes the object name where the other methods pass options.Kind. The candidate also notes the cardinality impact, but the underlying issue is identical.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request context and are cancelled when the HTTP handler returns

In Create (and identically in Delete line 110, Update line 135, DeleteCollection line 163) the fire-and-forget goroutine does context.WithTimeoutCause(ctx, 10s, ...) on the incoming request ctx. The request context is cancelled as soon as the API handler finishes writing the response, which typically happens immediately after the synchronous unified-storage write returns — long before the 10s timeout matters. The legacy write will therefore be aborted with context.Canceled in the common case (any legacy call slower than handler teardown), so the 'safe measure' legacy copy silently diverges from unified storage, with the failure only visible as a metric bump. The goroutine should derive from context.WithoutCancel(ctx) (or a detached background context carrying the logger/values) so the legacy write can actually complete.

Delete no longer attempts legacy deletion when unified storage returns NotFound

The previous implementation distinguished NotFound: if d.Storage.Delete returned an IsNotFound error it still went on to delete from Legacy, so objects that exist only in the legacy store (e.g., written before mode 3 was enabled, or whose legacy write succeeded while unified failed) could still be cleaned up. The new code returns immediately on any error from unified storage, so a Get in mode 3 would 404 while the object still exists in the legacy store, and there is no way through the dual writer to delete that orphaned legacy object. This leaves permanent legacy orphans during the migration window mode 3 is designed for.

Legacy Update re-derives the object from legacy's own old object instead of mirroring what unified storage stored

The previous mode 3 Update fetched the old object, computed the updated object once via objInfo.UpdatedObject, and used updateWrapper so that the legacy store persisted exactly the object returned by unified storage. The new code hands the raw objInfo to d.Legacy.Update inside the goroutine, so legacy's store invokes objInfo.UpdatedObject against legacy's own (possibly stale) old object. If legacy is behind unified storage (which is expected in mode 3, since legacy writes are async), the legacy update can conflict or produce a different object than what unified storage stored, and the resulting error is only counted in a metric — never logged and never surfaced. The legacy 'safety net' copy can thus silently and permanently drift from unified storage.

Fire-and-forget legacy writes can be applied out of order

Because every mutating operation spawns an independent goroutine for the legacy write with no sequencing, two rapid operations on the same object (e.g., Update then Delete, or two Updates) can be applied to the legacy store in the opposite order — the delete goroutine can run before the update goroutine, resurrecting the object in legacy, or an older update can overwrite a newer one. Since mode 3 treats legacy as the fallback store to migrate back to, this reordering can leave the legacy copy in a state that never matched unified storage. Some ordering mechanism (per-key queue, or at minimum synchronous ordering guarantees) is needed.

Create storage-error path records a legacy-duration metric

When d.Storage.Create fails, the code calls d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) even though no legacy call was ever made and the measured duration is the unified-storage create. It should be recordStorageDuration(true, ...). As written, unified-storage create failures are reported as legacy errors and the storage error metric is never incremented, making alerting on unified-storage failures blind to create errors.

Update storage-error path records a legacy-duration metric

When d.Storage.Update fails, d.recordLegacyDuration(true, mode3Str, options.Kind, method, startStorage) is called even though the failure came from unified storage and no legacy update was attempted. It should be recordStorageDuration(true, ...). Unified-storage update failures will be misattributed to legacy in the dual-writer metrics.

DeleteCollection legacy write records a storage-duration metric

Inside the DeleteCollection goroutine, the result of d.Legacy.DeleteCollection is recorded with d.recordStorageDuration(err != nil, ...) instead of recordLegacyDuration. Legacy delete-collection latency and failures are attributed to unified storage, and the legacy metric for this method is never populated.

Mode 3 integration tests assert legacy API state synchronously while legacy writes are asynchronous

doPlaylistTests contains checks like 'Do CRUD via k8s (and check that legacy api still works)' that write through the k8s API and immediately read via the legacy /api/playlists endpoints (getFromBothAPIs). In mode 3 the legacy write happens in a detached goroutine after the response is returned, so these assertions race with the legacy write: on a loaded CI worker the legacy GET can observe the pre-write state and fail intermittently (and combined with the request-context cancellation in dualwriter_mode3.go, the legacy write may never land at all). The mode 3 subtests need to poll/wait for the legacy state to converge instead of asserting it immediately.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In DualWriterMode3's DeleteCollection method, when a storage operation fails, recordStorageDuration is incorrectly called with recordLegacyDuration instead.

Either drop the `rulerRule` requirement from the render guard or pass the identifier through instead.

`useAllAlertRuleAbilities` (still used by existing components such as the old list's RuleActionsButtons via `useAlertRuleAbility`) previously computed `isFederated = isFederatedRuleGroup(rule.group)` and treated federated groups as immutable (no edit/delete). As a result, rules in federated Mimir rule groups (groups with `source_tenants`) are no longer marked immutable on this code path, so Edit/Delete buttons can be shown for rules that must not be modified through Grafana. In `useAllGrafanaPromRuleAbilities`, `[AlertRuleAction.ModifyExport]: [isAlertingRule, exportAllowed]` uses `prometheusRuleType.grafana.alertingRule(rule)`, which is false for recording rules. The ruler-based equivalent used `rulerRuleType.grafana.rule(rule)` (`isGrafanaRulerRule`), which is true for both alerting and recording rules. In the list view (no ruler rule available), `canExport` therefore becomes false for Grafana-managed recording rules and the Export menu item disappears, whereas previously recording rules could be exported from the list. The same `isAlertingRule` gating on Pause/Restore also diverges from the old semantics (Grafana recording rules support pausing). Use a check that includes recording rules where the action legitimately applies to them.

Rule view link no longer carries the returnTo parameter

The previous implementation built the rule link as `createRelativeUrl(`/alerting/grafana/${uid}/view`, { returnTo })` using `createReturnTo()`; the new `GrafanaRuleListItem` drops the `returnTo` parameter. Users navigating from the list to a rule's detail page will lose the 'return to previous' context, so going back from the detail view no longer returns them to their filtered list position. If this was not an intentional product change, restore the `returnTo` query parameter.

Stale comment and variable name still reference ruler rule preloading

The comment above the cache-preload block still says 'This is not mandatory to preload ruler rules, but it improves the UX / Because the user waits a bit longer for the initial load but doesn't need to wait for each group to be loaded', and the variable is still named `cacheAndRulerPreload`, but the `alertRuleApi.util.prefetch('getGrafanaRulerGroup', ...)` call was removed in this PR. The comment now describes behavior the code no longer has and is misleading to future readers; update the comment and rename the variable to reflect that only the Prometheus groups cache is populated.

Interpolating before the split decision defeats the $__range guard, so $__range queries are now split

runSplitQuery now maps every target through datasource.applyTemplateVariables before partition() calls querySupportsSplitting(). querySupportsSplitting (line 287) relies on isQueryWithRangeVariable(query.expr) matching the literal '$__range' in the raw expression to exclude those queries from time-based splitting — the comment above it states these queries must not be split because the range window would be computed incorrectly per chunk. Because applyTemplateVariables runs templateSrv.replace over the expression, '$__range' is resolved to a fixed duration (the full request range) before the check executes, so isQueryWithRangeVariable can never match anymore and queries like avg_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) or topk(...)[$__range] are now split into per-day chunks, each chunk carrying the same pre-baked full-range window. This silently produces incorrect merged results for exactly the class of queries the guard was created to protect. The split/non-split decision must be made on the original uninterpolated expression (e.g., partition before applying template variables, or check isQueryWithRangeVariable on the pre-interpolation expr).

Ad hoc filters are now injected multiple times into split queries

applyTemplateVariables is now called with request.filters as the third argument, which injects the ad hoc filter matchers into the selector at split-preparation time. However, every split sub-request is still executed through datasource.runQuery, which applies the same request.filters to its targets again when it calls applyTemplateVariables. In the shard-splitting path it is even worse: runShardSplitQuery (shardQuerySplitting.ts line 52) applies the filters, then runSplitQuery applies them again, then runQuery applies them a third time. With ad hoc filters configured and query splitting enabled, the expression sent to Loki contains the filter matchers duplicated two or three times, e.g. {job="x", cluster="us", cluster="us"}. This is semantically redundant, changes the query text (and therefore cache keys/history) compared to before this PR, and stacks multiple string-level insertions through the naive addAdhocFilters replacement. Filters should be applied in exactly one place in the execution chain.

No test that $__range queries remain excluded from splitting

The new tests only cover the happy path (variables like $__auto and $step are replaced before execution). The behavior most at risk from moving interpolation to the start of runSplitQuery — that queries containing '$__range' are still routed to the non-splitting path via querySupportsSplitting — has no coverage, and in fact no longer works. A test with an expression such as avg_over_time({a="b"}[$__range]) asserting that only a single, unsplit request is executed would have caught the regression introduced by interpolating before the split decision.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The applyTemplateVariables method is called with request.filters as the third parameter, but this parameter is not used in the corresponding test setup.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Count-then-insert limit check is racy and can exceed the configured device limit

CreateOrUpdateDevice enforces the limit by calling CountDevices and then, if count < deviceLimit, running the INSERT ... ON CONFLICT upsert. These are two separate statements with no transaction or locking, so N concurrent requests with distinct new device IDs can all observe count < limit and all insert, pushing the device table past deviceLimit. Since anonymous requests are unauthenticated and arrive concurrently (and each device is only cached locally per instance for 29 minutes, so multi-instance deployments re-check often), overshooting the limit under load is realistic. If the limit is meant as a hard cap, enforcement needs to be atomic (e.g., conditional insert in a transaction or a database-level constraint).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. Concurrent requests can each pass the count check before inserting, so the device limit can be exceeded. Both also suggest the same kind of fix: a transaction or atomic enforcement.

true_positives.golden_comment: The updateDevice function returns ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0, but zero affected rows means the device doesn't exist or falls outside the time window, not that a limit was reached.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
updateDevice can report ErrDeviceLimitReached for an existing device on MySQL

updateDevice treats `rowsAffected == 0` as 'device does not exist / not in window' and returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. On MySQL (grafana's DSN does not set clientFoundRows), RowsAffected counts rows actually changed, not rows matched. The UPDATE sets updated_at to the current time, but anon_device.updated_at has second precision on MySQL, so two tag refreshes for the same device within the same second with unchanged client_ip/user_agent produce no changed columns and rowsAffected == 0. An existing, in-window device then gets ErrDeviceLimitReached and its anonymous authentication fails even though it is already counted against the limit. Compare using a matched-rows semantic or restructure the check (e.g., SELECT the device first, or use CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS).
true_positives.reasoning: Both point at the same code: updateDevice returning ErrDeviceLimitReached when rowsAffected == 0. The golden says the error is semantically wrong because zero rows means the device doesn't exist or is outside the window, not that a limit was hit. The candidate makes a different argument: on MySQL, rowsAffected can be 0 for an existing device whose row was matched but not changed, so the error fires falsely. Still, both flag that rowsAffected == 0 is wrongly mapped to ErrDeviceLimitReached, so they overlap substantially.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `tagDeviceUI` function populates the local cache with the device ID before the `CreateOrUpdateDevice` call. If `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is returned, the cache entry remains set, allowing subsequent requests to bypass the device limit until the cache expires after 29 minutes.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Local cache is populated before the DB write, so the device limit is only enforced once per device

In tagDeviceUI, the cache key is set with `a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})` (line 87) before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is called. When the device limit is reached, CreateOrUpdateDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached, but the cache entry was already written and stays valid for ~29 minutes. On the next request from the same device, tagDeviceUI hits the cache at line 83-84 and returns nil without touching the database, so Anonymous.Authenticate (client.go) no longer sees ErrDeviceLimitReached and the request is allowed. Result: a new device over the limit is rejected exactly once, then gets full anonymous access for the rest of the cache window (and the window renews each time the device is re-tagged after expiry fails again). This effectively defeats the configurable device limit this PR adds. The cache entry should only be set after CreateOrUpdateDevice succeeds.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue. The cache is set before CreateOrUpdateDevice, the entry persists when ErrDeviceLimitReached is returned, and the device limit is bypassed for the ~29 minute cache window.

false_positives.candidate:
No test that an existing device can still be updated when the limit is reached

TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit only verifies that a *new* device is rejected with ErrDeviceLimitReached once the limit is reached. The other half of the feature — that a device already present in anon_device (and within the 30-day window) is still allowed via the updateDevice path when count >= deviceLimit — is untested. A regression that rejects existing devices at the limit (e.g., the MySQL rowsAffected issue, or a broken WHERE clause in updateDevice) would not be caught. Add a case: limit=1, create device A, then call CreateOrUpdateDevice again for device A and assert it succeeds and updates the row.

New device_limit option is not documented in the config files

The PR adds `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` under [auth.anonymous], but the changed-files list does not include conf/defaults.ini or conf/sample.ini, so the new `device_limit` option is undocumented and invisible to administrators browsing or generating config. Per Grafana convention, new ini options should be added (commented, with description) to conf/defaults.ini and conf/sample.ini; otherwise the feature is undiscoverable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Anonymous authentication now fails entirely if anonDeviceService.TagDevice returns ErrDeviceLimitReached. Previously, device tagging was asynchronous and non-blocking. This change prevents anonymous users from authenticating when the device limit is reached.

Time window calculation inconsistency: Using device.UpdatedAt.UTC().Add(-anonymousDeviceExpiration) as the lower bound but device.UpdatedAt as the current time may not match the intended logic. Consider using time.Now().UTC() consistently.

false_positives.candidate:
Fallback locales are only loaded for controller requests, so fallbacks silently fail in jobs/mailers

Fallback loading is triggered solely by `I18n.fallbacks.ensure_loaded!` in `ApplicationController#set_locale`. Because the translate accelerator lazy-loads only `config.locale` (see `translate` in lib/freedom_patches/translate_accelerator.rb), any translation performed outside a web request — Sidekiq jobs, user notification emails, scheduled tasks — will have the current locale's file loaded but never the fallback chain (site default locale and :en). In those contexts a key missing from the user's locale will render as 'translation missing' instead of falling back to the default/English string, so the feature only works for HTTP requests and silently no-ops elsewhere. The fallback loading should happen inside the translation path (e.g., in `load_locale`/`translate` or `I18n.with_locale`) rather than in a controller before_filter.

Translation LRU cache key does not account for the fallback chain, so cached results go stale when default_locale changes or differs per site

The accelerator caches no-argument translations under `"#{key}#{config.locale}#{config.backend.object_id}"`. Before this change, the translation for a given key+locale depended only on that locale's file; now it also depends on the fallback chain, which includes `SiteSetting.default_locale` (see `FallbackLocaleList#[]` in config/initializers/i18n.rb). The cache is only cleared by `I18n.reload!`, which a site-setting change does not trigger. Consequences: (1) after an admin changes the site default locale, keys missing in a user's locale keep serving strings from the old default locale until the process restarts; (2) on multisite installs where different sites share the process and backend but have different `default_locale` values, a fallback result cached for one site is served to another site with a different default locale, producing wrong-language output. The cache key needs to incorporate the effective fallback list (or the cache must be invalidated when `default_locale` changes).

FallbackLocaleList#[] recomputes the chain on every translation lookup

`I18n::Backend::Fallbacks#translate` calls `I18n.fallbacks[locale]` for every translation that reaches the backend (which is all translations with interpolation arguments, since the LRU cache only covers the no-args path). The overridden `[]` performs a `SiteSetting.default_locale` lookup, allocates a symbol via `to_sym`, allocates and `uniq`s an array on every call, even though the result only changes when `default_locale` changes. On translation-heavy pages this is pure per-call overhead. Consider memoizing the computed list and invalidating it when the default_locale setting changes.

No tests for the new fallback ordering and loading behavior

This PR introduces a custom fallback chain (user locale → site default locale → :en), replaces the global `I18n.fallbacks` object with a custom `FallbackLocaleList`, moves pluralization setup between initializers, and adds `ensure_loaded!` to the translation accelerator, but changes no spec files (the PR description is also just the placeholder 'Test 9'). There is no coverage verifying that a key missing in the user locale resolves to the default locale and then to English, that `FallbackLocaleList#[]` behaves correctly when the user locale equals the default locale, or that fallback locale files actually get loaded. A regression here would surface as untranslated UI strings and would be easy to miss without tests.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The @loaded_locales instance variable in translate_accelerator.rb is lazily initialized and accessed by multiple concurrent threads without synchronization.

Consider normalizing the input locale (e.g., to a symbol) when checking/loading here to avoid double-loading if the same locale is passed as a String vs Symbol (also applies to other locations in the PR).

true_positives.golden_comment: The traceID is no longer logged for plugin requests. During a refactoring, the tracing import and the logic to extract and add traceID from the context to log parameters were removed from the LoggerMiddleware. Nothing else in the middleware chain injects traceID as a contextual log attribute, so the traceID field that operators previously had for correlating these plugin request logs with traces silently disappears from the "Plugin Request Completed" log line whenever plugin_log_backend_requests is enabled. If traceID was intended to be kept, it should either be re-added explicitly to logParams or included in the contextual attributes by the ContextualLoggerMiddleware.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same issue as the golden comment. traceID was removed along with the tracing import, and the new ContextualLoggerMiddleware never adds it, so plugin request logs no longer carry traceID.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `TestLogger.FromContext` method returns a new `TestLogger` instance via `NewTestLogger()` instead of returning the receiver (f). This causes logs to be recorded on an un-referenced instance, leading to broken test assertions that expect logs to be recorded on the original logger.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
TestLogger.FromContext returns a new instance, discarding captured logs

TestLogger.FromContext ignores the receiver and returns NewTestLogger(), i.e. a fresh, empty TestLogger. Since LoggerMiddleware now logs through m.logger.FromContext(ctx).Info(...) instead of calling the injected logger directly, any test that passes a TestLogger and then asserts on its InfoLogs/WarnLogs fields will see zero calls — the log entry is recorded on the discarded instance, so the assertion fails (or, worse, if written to tolerate absence, silently passes). The fake should return the receiver itself (return f) so logs emitted through the FromContext path are captured on the same object the test holds.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug. TestLogger.FromContext returns NewTestLogger() instead of the receiver, so logs are recorded on a discarded instance and test assertions on the original logger break.

true_positives.golden_comment: The EmbeddableHost model's before_validation callback calls self.host.sub! to strip http://, https://, and path segments, but if self.host is nil, this raises NoMethodError.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
before_validation crashes with NoMethodError when host is nil

The `before_validation` block calls `self.host.sub!(...)` unconditionally. If an `EmbeddableHost` is built without a host (e.g. the admin controller receives a request missing `embeddable_host[host]`, or code does `EmbeddableHost.new.valid?`), `nil.sub!` raises NoMethodError, producing a 500 instead of a validation error. true_positives.golden_comment: The update and destroy methods in Admin::EmbeddableHostsController do not validate the existence of the EmbeddableHost record retrieved by ID. If EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first returns nil (i.e., the host does not exist), attempting to call methods on the nil object (e.g., save_host or destroy) will result in a NoMethodError.

update and destroy raise NoMethodError for an unknown host id instead of 404

`update` and `destroy` do `EmbeddableHost.where(id: params[:id]).first` and then use the result without a nil check: `update` passes nil into `save_host`, where `host.host = ...` raises NoMethodError, and `destroy` calls `host.destroy` on nil. A request for a deleted or bogus id returns a 500. Both actions should raise `Discourse::NotFound` (or use `find`) when the record is missing.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate describes the same bug as the golden comment. In the update and destroy actions, a nil host from where(id).first is used without a check, which raises NoMethodError.

true_positives.golden_comment: record_for_host compares lower(host) = ? but does not normalize the parameter’s case, so mixed‑case referer hosts may fail to match even though comparison intends to be case‑insensitive.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
record_for_host does not downcase the incoming host and cannot match hosts saved with a port

`record_for_host` runs `where("lower(host) = ?", host)` where `host` is `uri.host`. Ruby's URI parser preserves the case of the host (it is only downcased by `#normalize`), so a referer like `http://EVILTROUT.COM/page` will not match the stored lowercase `eviltrout.com` — the comparison should be against `host.downcase`. Additionally, the host validation regex on line 2 permits an optional port (`(:[0-9]{1,5})?`), so an admin can save `example.com:3000`, but `uri.host` strips the port, meaning such a record can never match and embedding from that host is always rejected. Either reject ports in validation or include the port in the lookup.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate explicitly says record_for_host compares lower(host) against an un-downcased host, so mixed-case referers fail to match. That is the same issue as the golden comment. The extra point about ports is additional and does not change the match.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because this migration inserts embeddable_hosts rows with raw SQL, any existing embeddable_hosts values that include http:// or /https:// or path segments won’t go through the EmbeddableHost model’s normalization, so the new host lookup (which compares only the bare host) may fail for migrated data. Consider ensuring that migrated hosts are normalized to the same format as newly created EmbeddableHost records so existing embedding configurations keep working.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migrated hosts are inserted raw, keeping scheme/path that lookups will never match

The old `embeddable_hosts` setting explicitly supported values like `http://discourse.org` and `https://example.com/1234` (the old specs set exactly those values). The new `EmbeddableHost` model strips the scheme and path in a `before_validation` callback, but the migration inserts the old values with raw SQL, bypassing the model entirely. After migration, rows contain e.g. `https://example.com/1234`, while `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` compares `uri.host` (`example.com`) against the stored value, so every previously configured host that included a scheme or path silently stops being allowed — existing embedded comment installs break until an admin manually re-saves each host.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same issue. The migration inserts hosts with raw SQL, which bypasses the model's normalization of scheme and path. Lookups compare only the bare host, so migrated entries fail to match.

VALUES ('#{h}', ...)"`. `h` comes from the `embeddable_hosts` site setting, which was free text; a host entry containing a single quote will produce invalid SQL and fail the migration mid-way (and in principle allows SQL injection). true_positives.golden_comment: The migration accesses execute(...)[0]['id'] without checking if the query returned any rows, which causes a crash when no embed_category setting exists. This can lead to a broken feature when attempting to edit category/host relationships.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Migration crashes when the embed_category site setting has no DB row

The migration does `execute("SELECT c.id FROM categories ... WHERE s.name = 'embed_category'")[0]['id']`. Site settings only have a row in the `site_settings` table when an admin has overridden the default; on any install where `embed_category` was never changed from its empty default (or was set to a blank/non-matching value so the join returns nothing), the result set is empty, `[0]` is nil, and `nil['id']` raises NoMethodError, aborting the migration and blocking the deploy. true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the migration indexing [0]['id'] on an empty result when the embed_category setting is missing, which crashes the migration. The candidate is the same issue with more detail.

false_positives.candidate:
No uniqueness constraint or validation on host

Neither the model nor the migration enforces uniqueness of `host`, so admins can create duplicate rows for the same host pointing at different categories. `EmbeddableHost.record_for_host` then uses `.first`, making the category chosen for imported embedded topics arbitrary, and the admin UI shows conflicting duplicate rows. Add a unique index plus `validates_uniqueness_of :host, case_sensitive: false`.

Plural *_ids hydration produces arrays of undefined and deletes the raw ids even when nothing was resolved

In `_hydrateEmbedded`, the new plural branch maps `foo_ids` through `_lookupSubType` and then unconditionally sets `obj[plural] = hydrated` and deletes `obj[k]`. Unlike the singular branch (which only assigns and deletes when a hydrated object was actually found), this branch assigns even when `_lookupSubType` returned undefined for some or all ids — producing e.g. `colors: [undefined, undefined]` and destroying the original `color_ids` data. Any payload containing a plural id array whose collection is missing from the root (or partially missing ids) is silently corrupted. It should skip the assignment when nothing resolved, and ideally compact/filter unresolved ids; the `|| []` on the map result is also dead code since `map` always returns an array.

New admin endpoints have no request specs

The specs added for `Admin::EmbeddableHostsController` (and `Admin::EmbeddingController`) only assert the class is a subclass of AdminController. There is no coverage for create/update/destroy behavior — authorization (non-staff rejected), the default-to-uncategorized category fallback, validation error rendering, deleting a host, or the embedding show endpoint. These endpoints implement the core of the feature (including the nil-record crashes noted above) and currently have zero functional coverage.

true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same core issue: include_website_name lacks the '?' suffix, so the conditional inclusion never applies. It does not mention the string mutation point, but the primary issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:

The example domains differ, but the underlying issue is identical. One detail is off in the candidate: `discourseUrl.indexOf(e.origin)` checks whether e.origin is a substring of discourseUrl, not the reverse, so its exact example is inaccurate. It still identifies the same flawed check.

true_positives.golden_comment: Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

i.content is nil for feeds without content:encoded, crashing the hourly job

Plain RSS 2.0 feeds that only provide `<description>` — which is extremely common — will have `i.content == nil`, so `i.content.scrub` raises NoMethodError. The exception aborts the whole PollFeed run (and since it is raised inside the hourly scheduled job, every subsequent run fails the same way), so no topics are ever imported from such feeds. The code should fall back to `i.description` when `i.content` is blank.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: `i.content` is nil for feeds that have no content field, so `i.content.scrub` crashes. Both also propose falling back to `description`.

false_positives.candidate:
RSS/feed HTML is stored and rendered without any sanitization (stored XSS)

poll_feed takes the raw HTML from each feed item (`CGI.unescapeHTML(i.content.scrub)`) and passes it to TopicEmbed.import, which creates the post with `cook_method: Post.cook_methods[:raw_html]`. Post#cook (app/models/post.rb) returns `raw` verbatim for raw_html posts, skipping the entire rendering and sanitization pipeline, and app/views/embed/best.html.erb renders it with `<%= raw post.cooked %>` (the main app also serves cooked HTML to clients). Nothing ever sanitizes this content, so a feed entry containing `<script>` or event-handler attributes becomes stored XSS executed for every forum visitor and embed viewer. The forum trusts the configured feed URL, but a compromised or hostile blog feed would fully compromise the forum. The imported HTML should be run through Sanitize (already a dependency) before being stored.

Per-URL retrieval throttle is trivially bypassed, enabling unauthenticated fetch amplification

The anonymous-accessible GET /embed/best endpoint enqueues a RetrieveTopic job for any embed_url, which makes the server perform an outbound HTTP fetch of that URL (TopicRetriever -> TopicEmbed.import_remote -> open(url)). The only protection is a 60-second Redis throttle keyed on the exact URL string (`retrieved:#{@embed_url}`). An attacker can bypass it indefinitely by appending unique query strings (e.g. ?r=1, ?r=2, ...) to the same page on the embeddable host, causing the forum to hammer the configured embeddable host with unbounded fetches — a denial-of-service amplification against the very site the forum operator embeds. The throttle should be normalized (e.g. keyed on host/path, or a global rate limit) and import_remote should have timeouts and size limits.

This migration was already merged and run by existing installations; changing `create_table :top_topics` to `create_table :top_topics, force: true` will never execute for anyone who already migrated, so whatever problem the edit was meant to fix silently persists for them. Worse, `force: true` drops the existing table before recreating it — for any environment where this migration has not yet run but the table exists with data, running it will destroy that data. If the table needs to be recreated, that must be done in a new migration.

Check-then-create race in TopicEmbed.import crashes concurrent jobs

import looks up `TopicEmbed.where(embed_url: url).first` and, when absent, creates the topic, post, and TopicEmbed row inside a transaction. Two RetrieveTopic jobs (or a poll plus a retrieve) for the same URL running concurrently can both see no existing embed and both try to create; the unique index on topic_embeds.embed_url makes the loser's `TopicEmbed.create!` raise ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique, rolling back the just-created topic/post and failing the Sidekiq job (with retries). The race should be handled, e.g. by rescuing RecordNotUnique and re-reading the existing embed.

absolutize_urls mangles protocol-relative URLs

URLs like `//cdn.example.com/img.png` start with '/', so they match the `href.start_with?('/')` branch and are rewritten to `http://<feed host>//cdn.example.com/img.png`, which is broken. Protocol-relative hrefs and srcs are common in feed content; they will all 404 after import. The rewrite should skip values starting with '//'.

`add_column :posts, :cook_method, :integer, default: 1, null: false` on PostgreSQL versions prior to 11 rewrites the entire posts table to materialize the default, taking an access-exclusive lock for the duration. On a large forum this can block all reads/writes to posts for a long time during deploy. The safer pattern for that era is to add the column without a default, backfill in batches, then set the default and NOT NULL constraint.

setnx + expire is not atomic; a crash between them permanently blocks retrieval of the URL

retrieved_recently? does `$redis.setnx(retrieved_key, "1")` followed by `$redis.expire(retrieved_key, 60)` as two separate commands. If the process crashes or the Redis connection drops between the two, the key is set with no TTL, and that embed URL will be treated as 'retrieved recently' forever — the topic will never be imported. A single atomic SET with EX (or setex) avoids the window.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The PollFeed job calls open(SiteSetting.feed_polling_url) without validating the URL, allowing an attacker who controls the feed_polling_url site setting to make the server fetch arbitrary internal or external URLs.
postMessage targetOrigin should be the origin (scheme+host+port), not the full referrer URL; using the full URL will cause the message to be dropped and prevent resizing.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.

The TopicEmbed.import method is susceptible to a NoMethodError if the contents parameter is nil when attempting to append a string, and an XSS vulnerability due to unescaped url interpolation in the generated HTML.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

The second definition, which expects a single dimensions string parameter, overrides the first, which expected separate max_width and max_height parameters. This makes the original method unreachable and breaks existing code that calls it with separate width and height arguments.

Client-side upload size validation hardcoded to 10 MB, ignoring configured per-type limits

`validateUploadedFile` previously enforced `Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb']`, so the composer blocked oversized files before upload using the admin-configured image/attachment limits. It now uses a hardcoded `10 * 1024`. On sites with lower configured limits, users pass client validation and only fail later with a server error; on sites with higher limits (e.g. large attachments allowed), users are incorrectly blocked at 10 MB. The error message also now interpolates the raw value 10240 as `max_size_kb`. false_positives.candidate:

The new downsize path calls `OptimizedImage.downsize(tempfile.path, tempfile.path, "80%", allow_animation: SiteSetting.allow_animated_thumbnails)`. Inside `OptimizedImage.optimize`, the animated branch is chosen only when `from =~ /\.GIF$/i`, but `from` here is the upload tempfile path (e.g. `/tmp/RackMultipart...`), which has no file extension, so the regex never matches. The code therefore falls through to `downsize_instructions`, which runs `convert #{from}[0] ...` — the `[0]` selector flattens the image to its first frame. A user uploading a large animated GIF will have the animation permanently discarded with no warning, even though `allow_animation` was explicitly passed. The animated-detection should be based on the original filename/content type, not the tempfile path.

The loop `while attempt > 0 && tempfile.size > SiteSetting.max_image_size_kb.kilobytes` never checks the boolean return value of `OptimizedImage.downsize`. If the conversion fails (corrupt image, unsupported format such as SVG written to an extensionless tempfile path so ImageMagick cannot determine the output format, missing binary), each iteration simply re-runs the same failing `convert` plus `ImageOptim` up to 5 times, wasting CPU in the deferred job and logging nothing about the upload-level failure. This branch handles any upload `type`, not just images, so an admin who raised `max_attachment_size_kb` above 10 MB still cannot pull larger files via the API URL flow (the download is silently truncated/rejected at 10 MB and `rescue nil` swallows it, yielding a confusing nil-tempfile failure), while an admin who lowered limits gets no benefit from the cap at this layer. If the intent was only to accommodate images that will later be downsized, the limit should still derive from a setting (or at least only relax for image types).

In `displayErrorForUpload`, the 413 handler now shows `I18n.t('post.errors.file_too_large', { max_size_kb: 10 * 1024 })` instead of `Discourse.SiteSettings.max_image_size_kb`. `tu = TopicUser.find_by(user_id: current_user.id, topic_id: params[:topic_id])` can return nil — any logged-in user can visit `/t/<id>/unsubscribe` for a topic they have never read, posted in, or been emailed about, in which case no topic_users row exists. false_positives.candidate: Unsubscribe mutates state on a GET request (CSRF / link-prefetch) The new `unsubscribe` action is routed as GET (`get "t/:topic_id/unsubscribe"` in config/routes.rb) and is added to `skip_before_filter :check_xhr`, so a plain browser GET with only the session cookie changes the user's TopicUser notification_level. The client then runs topic-from-params' setupController with a garbage nearPost, loading the topic stream instead of the unsubscribe confirmation page. The route must be declared before the topic resource (or nested with an explicit path that takes precedence).

unsubscribe_link translation now requires unsubscribe_url; callers without it will raise

config/locales/server.en.yml changed `unsubscribe_link` to include `[click here](%{unsubscribe_url})`. Any existing or future caller that sets `add_unsubscribe_link: true` without `unsubscribe_url` will now raise I18n::MissingInterpolationArgument and fail to build the email.
